Multimodal MRI can reveal coordinated remodeling of the heart-brain axis at the macroscopic structural level. CMR, currently regarded as the gold standard for assessing cardiac structure, function, and tissue characteristics, enables comprehensive evaluation of ventricular remodeling, myocardial fibrosis, edema, and perfusion abnormalities through techniques such as cine MRI, LGE, and T1/T2 mapping. Among these techniques, cine MRI enables accurate quantification of ventricular volumes, ejection fraction, and myocardial strain. LGE is widely used to identify focal fibrosis and scar formation, whereas T1/T2 mapping and extracellular volume fraction (ECV) measurements allow quantitative assessment of diffuse myocardial fibrosis and tissue remodeling (13). Correspondingly, structural brain MRI, including T1-weighted and T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging, can detect representative cerebral injury phenotypes such as brain atrophy, cerebral infarction, and white matter hyperintensities (WMHs) (14). An increasing number of studies have demonstrated significant associations between cardiac remodeling and structural brain abnormalities. For example, patients with heart failure frequently exhibit reduced gray matter volume (15) in regions including the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and cingulate cortex, whereas patients with atrial fibrillation (16) or cardiomyopathy frequently exhibit cerebral small vessel disease markers, including increased WMH burden and silent cerebral infarction and manifestations of cerebral small vessel disease (17). These findings suggest that cardiac and cerebral injuries are not isolated events (14) but rather components of a systemic remodeling process jointly driven by chronic hypoperfusion, vascular remodeling, and autonomic imbalance (18).

Therefore, structural MRI is valuable not only for identifying single-organ injury, but also for providing critical imaging evidence to characterize “structural co-remodeling” within the heart-brain axis. This approach is gradually shifting research on heart-brain comorbidities from the description of localized lesions toward cross-organ systemic phenotyping and integrative network-based analysis (19). Current evidence regarding the temporal sequence and causal direction of heart-brain remodeling remains limited. Most available studies are cross-sectional in nature and primarily demonstrate concurrent associations between cardiac abnormalities, such as reduced myocardial strain, ventricular remodeling, and myocardial fibrosis, and cerebral alterations, including white matter hyperintensities, hippocampal atrophy, and disrupted functional connectivity. However, longitudinal MRI studies capable of determining whether cardiac remodeling precedes cerebral injury, or conversely whether cerebral alterations contribute to subsequent cardiac dysfunction, remain scarce (20).

Beyond macroscopic structural alterations, diffusion MRI further reveals microstructural network injury within the heart-brain axis (21). Techniques such as diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), DTI, and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) enable multidimensional assessment of cerebral microstructural abnormalities, including white matter fiber integrity, axonal density, and neural network organization. In heart-brain axis research, these techniques are particularly valuable for evaluating the structural integrity of the CAN (22). The CAN primarily includes the insular cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, thalamus, and brainstem, and is responsible for integrating emotional, cognitive, and visceral autonomic information (22). DTI studies have shown that patients with heart failure and neurodegenerative diseases commonly exhibit reduced white matter integrity within frontolimbic systems and brainstem autonomic pathways (23), characterized by decreased fractional anisotropy and increased mean diffusivity (24). These findings indicate disruption of autonomic regulatory networks, which may further contribute to sympathetic-parasympathetic imbalance and abnormal cardiovascular regulation. In addition, microstructural MRI provides important mechanistic insights into how progressive degeneration of brain networks may contribute to cardiovascular dysfunction. For example, in patients with Parkinson's disease and AD (25), abnormalities in white matter connectivity are associated not only with cognitive decline, but also with reduced heart rate variability and impaired blood pressure regulation (26). These findings suggest that degeneration of autonomic neural networks may represent a critical mechanistic link between neurodegenerative pathology and cardiovascular dysfunction.

Therefore, diffusion MRI is shifting heart-brain axis research from conventional anatomical observation toward the evaluation of “network integrity” (22) and provides important imaging evidence for understanding the role of the autonomic nervous system in cross-organ information transfer and systemic network dysregulation.

fMRI further elucidates the dynamic regulatory mechanisms of the heart-brain axis from the perspective of functional connectivity. In particular, resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) enables assessment of functional synchronization among distributed brain regions in the absence of task performance, thereby facilitating the identification of brain network abnormalities associated with autonomic regulation. Current evidence suggests that the default mode network (DMN), salience network, and limbic system constitute key neural substrates involved in heart-brain axis regulation (27). Among these networks, the insula-anterior cingulate cortex pathway is considered a critical hub for autonomic control, and its dysfunction is closely associated with sympathetic overactivation, reduced heart rate variability, and impaired emotional regulation. Functional connectivity abnormalities within these networks have been observed in patients with heart failure and psychiatric disorders (28), suggesting that distinct disease states may share common mechanisms of heart-brain coupling (29). Importantly, rs-fMRI has shifted heart-brain axis research from the analysis of focal lesions toward the investigation of network-level dysfunction (30). Increasing evidence indicates that cardiovascular abnormalities affect not only regional cerebral perfusion but also induce widespread reorganization of functional brain networks. For example, patients with chronic heart failure frequently exhibit reduced connectivity between the DMN and executive control network (28), whereas patients with anxiety and depression more commonly demonstrate salience network hyperactivation and abnormal limbic coupling (31). These findings suggest that functional brain network remodeling may represent a key neural basis underlying heart-brain comorbidities.

Perfusion MRI provides an important tool for characterizing hemodynamic abnormalities within the heart-brain axis. ASL enables noninvasive quantification of cerebral blood flow, whereas dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) allows further assessment of blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity and microvascular permeability (32). Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion is considered a key mechanism linking cardiovascular disease and brain dysfunction (14). Studies have shown that patients with heart failure and atrial fibrillation often exhibit reduced cerebral perfusion globally, as well as in critical regions such as the hippocampus, and these reductions are associated with the severity of cognitive impairment (23). These findings suggest that persistent reductions in cardiac output, together with impaired cerebral autoregulation, may jointly contribute to structural and network-level brain injury. In addition, following stroke or acute brain injury, excessive sympathetic activation and inflammatory responses can lead to endothelial dysfunction and increased BBB permeability. DCE-MRI studies have demonstrated that BBB disruption not only contributes to acute neuroinflammatory responses but may also promote subsequent white matter injury and long-term cognitive decline (33). Furthermore, patients with neurodegenerative diseases also exhibit impaired neurovascular coupling (34), suggesting that dysregulation of cerebral blood flow represents a shared pathological mechanism across multiple heart-brain comorbid conditions.

Therefore, perfusion MRI not only enables the assessment of focal ischemia but also provides critical insight into dynamic blood flow-vascular-neural interactions within the heart-brain axis (34), offering an important framework for understanding chronic hypoperfusion and cerebrovascular dysfunction in heart-brain comorbidities.

With the development of metabolic MRI, heart-brain axis research has expanded beyond structural and functional characterization toward molecular and metabolic investigation of cross-organ interactions (35). Advanced techniques, including MRS multinuclear MRI (31P-MRS and 23Na MRI), and quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM), enable in vivo assessment of key biological processes, such as energy metabolism, ionic homeostasis, oxidative stress, and metal deposition (36). Increasing clinical evidence suggests that these approaches can identify metabolic signatures associated with both cardiovascular and neurological disorders, thereby providing new insights into the biological mechanisms underlying heart-brain coupling.

Among these techniques, 31P-MRS has been extensively applied in patients with heart failure and ischemic cardiomyopathy, demonstrating reduced phosphocreatine-to-adenosine triphosphate (PCr/ATP) ratios, which indicate impaired myocardial energy metabolism and mitochondrial dysfunction (37). Importantly, these metabolic abnormalities may occur before overt structural remodeling, highlighting the potential value of 31P-MRS as an early biomarker of myocardial dysfunction (38). Similarly, 23Na MRI provides unique information regarding myocardial sodium homeostasis disturbances in ischemic and fibrotic tissues, offering a potential non-invasive approach for assessing myocardial ionic dysregulation associated with injury and remodeling.

Metabolic MRI has also provided important evidence of brain metabolic alterations associated with cardiovascular diseases. Brain MRS studies in patients with heart failure and cognitive impairment have demonstrated abnormal metabolite profiles, including reduced N-acetylaspartate levels and disrupted neurotransmitter-related metabolism, suggesting neuronal dysfunction secondary to cardiac impairment (39). Furthermore, QSM has revealed abnormal iron accumulation in neurodegenerative disorders such as AD and Parkinson's disease, with increased iron deposition associated with disease progression and cognitive decline (40, 41). These findings suggest that metabolic and molecular imaging may provide a valuable framework for investigating the interplay between vascular dysfunction, neurodegeneration, and heart-brain axis disorders.

Beyond MRI-based metabolic imaging, positron emission tomography (PET) provides complementary molecular information regarding glucose metabolism, inflammation, and protein deposition through disease-specific radiotracers (42). ^18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-PET has demonstrated abnormal metabolic remodeling in cardiovascular diseases and characteristic cerebral metabolic patterns in neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease. Moreover, hybrid PET/MRI platforms enable simultaneous assessment of cardiac remodeling, cerebral metabolism, inflammation, and molecular alterations, offering a comprehensive approach for investigating the complex biological mechanisms of heart-brain interactions (43).

In recent years, MRI research has evolved from single-organ assessment toward integrated cross-organ imaging. One-stop heart-brain MRI enables simultaneous acquisition of cardiac and cerebral structural, functional, and perfusion information within a single examination, allowing systematic evaluation of dynamic interactions along the heart-brain axis. Studies combining (ECG), electroencephalography, and MRI have demonstrated temporal synchronization between brain activity and cardiac rhythms. By integrating brain functional connectivity, heart rate variability, and autonomic nervous system indices (27), it is possible to construct dynamic brain-heart coupling models that characterize directional information flow and temporal evolution across different disease states. Meanwhile, advances in graph theory analysis and network neuroscience have driven a shift in heart-brain axis research from localized abnormalities toward system-level network modeling. Metrics such as nodal centrality, modularity, and global efficiency enable quantitative assessment of information integration capacity and dynamic organizational properties between brain networks and the cardiovascular system.

In addition, developments in flexible coil technology, ultra-high-field MRI (44), and deep learning-based reconstruction algorithms have further improved spatial resolution and scanning efficiency, making integrated brain-heart imaging increasingly feasible. These advances may enable continuous, cross-organ, and multi-timescale dynamic observation, providing a new paradigm for elucidating directional propagation and system-level coupling mechanisms within the heart-brain axis.

Multimodal MRI reveals cross-organ coupling mechanisms in heart-brain axis disorders
Multimodal MRI has emerged as a powerful tool for investigating the heart-brain axis by providing comprehensive assessments of structural, functional, vascular, and metabolic alterations in both organs. Through the integration of cardiac and cerebral imaging biomarkers, it enables the evaluation of bidirectional heart-brain interactions and offers mechanistic insights into the processes underlying co-remodeling and co-atrophy. Across representative heart-brain disorders, converging multimodal MRI evidence has revealed recurring cross-organ imaging signatures. Abnormal insular functional connectivity is frequently associated with impaired myocardial strain, whereas hippocampal atrophy and white matter injury commonly accompany myocardial fibrosis and adverse cardiac remodeling (39). These reproducible imaging phenotypes support the concept that heart and brain dysfunction evolve through interconnected autonomic, vascular, inflammatory, and metabolic pathways, highlighting the unique value of multimodal MRI for characterizing systemic heart-brain coupling.

Acute brain injuries such as ischemic stroke can rapidly induce significant cardiac dysfunction (45), representing a classic brain-to-heart pathological pattern. The underlying mechanisms are primarily related to injury of key autonomic regulatory centers, including the insular cortex, thalamus, and brainstem (46), which triggers a sympathetic storm and catecholamine-mediated cardiotoxicity (45). Acute brain injury also activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (45), leading to excessive catecholamine release. This cascade contributes to neurogenic myocardial injury, myocardial stunning, and microcirculatory dysfunction. In addition, catecholamine surge can disrupt intracellular calcium homeostasis and impair mitochondrial function in cardiomyocytes, ultimately resulting in apical ballooning of the left ventricle, known as Takotsubo syndrome (TTS) (47). This neuro-cardiac interaction is characterized by a dynamic and bidirectional relationship. On one hand, excessive sympathetic activation may further aggravate cardiac injury through neurogenic myocardial edema and inflammatory responses. On the other hand, reduced cardiac output caused by myocardial stunning can exacerbate cerebral hypoperfusion, thereby worsening ischemic brain injury and creating a vicious cycle of injury propagation. Cardiac dysfunction following stroke represents one of the most representative models of acute neurogenic myocardial injury in heart-brain axis research and has recently been conceptualized as stroke-heart syndrome (48). Epidemiological studies have shown that patients with TTS have a significantly increased risk of stroke (49), while the incidence of TTS in patients with acute ischemic stroke is approximately 1.2% (47), suggesting a close bidirectional pathological relationship between the two conditions. In patients undergoing both cardiac and brain MRI, typical imaging features of TTS may coexist with stroke-related cerebral lesions, further supporting the presence of brain-heart coupling (50). The insular cortex, as a key autonomic regulatory hub, may trigger excessive sympathetic activation and myocardial injury when affected by ischemia (46). In addition, brainstem ischemia-related autonomic dysfunction is also considered an important mechanism underlying acute neurogenic cardiac injury. Conversely, cardiac disorders such as atrial fibrillation and heart failure can further increase the risk of stroke and cerebral hypoperfusion, forming a sustained heart-brain pathological cascade (51). MRI plays a crucial role in elucidating stroke-related cardiac injury. Brain MRI, particularly DWI, FLAIR, and perfusion imaging, enables precise delineation of ischemic core and penumbra (52). Lesions involving the insula, thalamus, and brainstem are closely associated with arrhythmias, myocardial injury, and hemodynamic instability, as these regions are directly involved in baroreflex regulation and autonomic output (52). Damage to these structures can rapidly disrupt the balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic activity. Notably, some ischemic stroke patients may present with DWI-negative findings (53), which are generally associated with relatively favorable clinical outcomes. On the cardiac side, CMR can identify characteristic features of TTS (54), including regional wall motion abnormalities, myocardial edema, and the absence of obstructive coronary artery disease. Techniques such as T1/T2 mapping and LGE further enable quantitative assessment of myocardial tissue alteration and microvascular injury. Overall, this brain injury-triggered cardiac response reflects, at its core, catecholamine-mediated neurogenic myocardial toxicity and acute microcirculatory dysfunction occurring on a short temporal scale (48).

Heart failure(HF) is a common clinical disease characterized by a decrease in the blood supply of the heart due to anatomical or functional problems with the heart. In China, studies on the epidemiology of HF have revealed an increase in the prevalence rate among people over 35, from 0.9% in 2000 to 1.3% in 2019 (57). Ischemic cardiomyopathy and hypertension are considered major causes of HF and are associated with cognitive function. Decreased systolic function of the heart and blood redistribution are symptoms of HF, which is frequently a subsequent condition to myocardial infarction (58, 59). The fundamental etiology of brain functional injury is thought to be the decrease in cerebral perfusion pressure brought on by decreased cardiac output and inflammation worsened by oxidative stress (60, 61). Although anatomical abnormalities in the brain were linked to biomarkers of myocardial injury and cardiac failure, only older people with poorer cognitive reserves displayed cognitive deficits (62, 63). Conventional MRI is only applicable to lesions with significant brain structure and cannot fully identify the pathological mechanism. White matter hyperintensity (WMH) was connected to sorrow and anxiety, and atrophy of the medial temporal lobe was connected to cognitive problems such as memory loss and executive dysfunction in HF patients. Reduced hippocampal volume is present in HF patients, which may contribute to depression and short-term memory loss (64). fMRI further evaluates neural activity and functional connectivity by measuring blood oxygenation and cerebral blood flow changes, revealing reduced activation in autonomic and cognitive regulatory regions such as the insula, hypothalamus, anterior cingulate cortex, cerebellum, and hippocampus (58), which may contribute to impaired attention, emotional regulation, and working memory in HF. Structural MRI (sMRI), particularly when combined with advanced analytical techniques such as voxel-based morphometry and surface-based morphometry, enables quantitative assessment of gray matter density, cortical thickness, and white matter integrity, demonstrating widespread gray matter loss in the medial temporal lobe, hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and precuneus that correlates with cognitive decline and HF severity (65, 66). In addition, WMH detected on T2-weighted or FLAIR imaging is closely associated with impaired information processing speed and executive dysfunction (67, 68). Cerebral perfusion imaging, including ASL, provides a noninvasive assessment of cerebral blood flow and microcirculation, showing reduced perfusion in the frontal cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, parietal lobe, and cerebellum of HF patients (58), suggesting that chronic cerebral hypoperfusion may contribute to neuronal injury and cognitive deterioration. Overall, the integration of conventional MRI, fMRI, sMRI, and perfusion imaging offers a comprehensive framework for understanding the heart-brain interaction in HF-associated cognitive impairment and may improve early diagnosis, mechanistic exploration, and therapeutic monitoring (15).

Representative multimodal MRI findings of heart failure-associated brain injury and cognitive impairment are illustrated in Figure 4. In patients with heart failure, reduced cardiac output and chronic hemodynamic impairment may result in sustained cerebral hypoperfusion and progressive neurovascular dysfunction. Functional MRI and advanced imaging analyses reveal alterations in large-scale cognitive and autonomic regulatory networks. Collectively, these multimodal MRI signatures provide imaging evidence of chronic heart-brain coupling and highlight the impact of cardiovascular dysfunction on cerebral structure, perfusion, and functional network organization.

Neurodegenerative diseases such as AD are characterized by progressive neuronal loss, disruption of large-scale neural networks, and chronic autonomic dysfunction. Increasing evidence suggests that AD is frequently accompanied by cardiovascular abnormalities, including impaired heart rate variability, autonomic imbalance, arrhythmias, and subclinical myocardial dysfunction, indicating chronic remodeling along the heart-brain axis. Research by Aili Toyli and colleagues has increasingly illuminated a complex, bidirectional relationship between cardiovascular disease and AD (70). Unlike acute brain injury-related cardiac dysfunction, neurodegeneration-associated heart-brain remodeling develops gradually and is characterized by chronic neurovascular dysfunction, persistent autonomic dysregulation, cerebral hypoperfusion, and progressive network reorganization. Multimodal MRI provides important insights into the structural, functional, and neurovascular mechanisms underlying these chronic interactions. Structural MRI studies consistently demonstrate hippocampal and medial temporal lobe atrophy in AD (71, 72), often accompanied by increased white matter hyperintensities, suggesting concomitant cerebral small vessel disease and chronic ischemic injury (73). ASL further reveals reduced cerebral blood flow in temporoparietal and posterior cingulate regions, closely associated with cognitive decline. DTI and NODDI show reduced white matter integrity and axonal density, particularly within hippocampal-prefrontal and limbic pathways. fMRI studies further demonstrate disrupted connectivity within the DMN, salience network, and memory-related circuits, with DMN dysfunction considered a hallmark imaging feature of AD. Importantly, DTI and fMRI can detect structural and functional abnormalities before overt clinical symptoms, supporting their value in early diagnosis (74). In addition to cerebral abnormalities, patients with AD frequently exhibit autonomic and cardiovascular dysfunction, including reduced heart rate variability, impaired baroreflex sensitivity, orthostatic hypotension, and altered sympathetic-parasympathetic balance. Chronic autonomic dysregulation may further impair cerebral perfusion and vascular homeostasis, thereby forming a vicious cycle between neurodegeneration and cardiovascular dysfunction. CMR studies also suggest the presence of subclinical myocardial remodeling and impaired cardiac function in some patients with AD (75). Recent advances in multimodal MRI and artificial intelligence have further improved the diagnostic and predictive capability of neuroimaging in AD. The integration of structural MRI, ASL, DTI, rs-fMRI, MRS, and machine learning enables multidimensional assessment of brain atrophy, perfusion deficits, white matter degeneration, metabolic abnormalities, and network dysfunction, providing promising tools for early diagnosis, longitudinal monitoring, and precision intervention in AD-related heart-brain axis remodeling (76, 77).

In neurodegenerative disorders, chronic neuronal loss and progressive disruption of large-scale brain networks may gradually impair autonomic regulation and contribute to cardiovascular dysfunction. Alzheimer's disease provides a representative model of this chronic brain-to-heart interaction, in which structural degeneration, perfusion abnormalities, and functional network disruption coexist with autonomic and cardiovascular alterations. Multimodal MRI enables comprehensive characterization of these cross-organ changes, revealing the complex relationship between neurodegeneration and cardiovascular remodeling (Figure 5) (78–81).

Current challenges and future perspectives
Although multimodal magnetic resonance imaging has advanced heart-brain axis research from single-organ assessment toward cross-organ systemic characterization, the field remains largely transitional between correlation-based observation, mechanistic inference, and clinical translation. Current limitations include insufficient causal inference, the predominance of cross-sectional studies, limited multimodal integration, and incomplete characterization of dynamic heart-brain coupling. In addition, the lack of standardized acquisition protocols and unified cross-scale analytical frameworks across structural, functional, perfusion, metabolic, and ultra-high-field MRI restricts reproducibility and cross-center generalizability (82).

Artificial intelligence is increasingly reshaping heart-brain axis imaging research from experience-driven interpretation toward data-driven systems modeling. Radiomics and deep learning enable quantitative characterization of complex imaging phenotypes and improve disease classification and risk prediction. Emerging graph neural networks and Transformer-based models further facilitate cross-organ network analysis by capturing nonlinear interactions among brain networks, cardiac remodeling, and autonomic regulation. However, current AI applications remain limited by insufficient interpretability, inadequate external validation, and weak integration with biological mechanisms, which constrain clinical translation (83).

Molecular imaging represents another promising direction for future heart-brain axis research (84). Although MRI provides excellent structural, functional, and metabolic characterization, molecular imaging modalities such as PET offer unique advantages in detecting cellular metabolism, neuroinflammation, protein aggregation, and receptor-specific alterations (85, 86). The integration of PET with MRI may provide complementary molecular, anatomical, and functional information, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of heart-brain interactions (87). Future development of hybrid PET/MRI platforms, combined with advanced MRI techniques and artificial intelligence-based image fusion methods, may facilitate characterization of disease processes from molecular abnormalities to organ-level remodeling (88).

Large-scale cohorts such as the UK Biobank further support integrative analyses combining multimodal MRI with genetic, physiological, and clinical data (89). The incorporation of genome-wide association studies and Mendelian randomization approaches may strengthen causal inference and improve mechanistic understanding of heart-brain interactions (90, 91). Although observational MRI studies have demonstrated significant associations between cardiac remodeling and cerebral structural alterations, causal inference remains limited. Emerging Mendelian randomization approaches provide a promising framework for investigating directional heart-brain interactions through the integration of genome-wide association study data derived from cardiac and brain MRI phenotypes. Future bidirectional MR analyses may help determine whether genetically predicted cardiac traits, such as left ventricular mass, myocardial fibrosis, and ventricular dysfunction, causally contribute to hippocampal atrophy, cortical thinning, and white matter injury. Such studies may further clarify the directionality of heart-brain interactions and advance mechanistic understanding of the heart-brain axis (92).

Although multimodal MRI provides a comprehensive framework for characterizing heart-brain interactions, its translation into routine clinical practice remains challenging. Advanced approaches, including quantitative MRI, multinuclear MRI, metabolic imaging, and integrated heart-brain imaging protocols, are currently available mainly in specialized centers due to limited accessibility, heterogeneous acquisition strategies, and the lack of standardized protocols. Beyond technical availability, clinical implementation also requires streamlined scanning workflows, effective multidisciplinary collaboration, and automated analysis platforms to enhance operational efficiency and clinical feasibility. Moreover, the substantial costs associated with advanced imaging technologies, specialized hardware, and computational infrastructure emphasize the importance of identifying high-risk populations who are most likely to benefit from these approaches. Large-scale prospective and multicenter studies are therefore needed to validate clinical utility, determine prognostic value, and assess cost-effectiveness before widespread adoption in routine care and reimbursement frameworks. Overcoming these challenges through technological innovation, protocol harmonization, and collaborative research efforts will be critical for translating heart-brain axis imaging from an emerging research tool into a practical approach for personalized risk stratification and precision medicine.

Future research should therefore emphasize longitudinal cohort designs, standardized multimodal imaging protocols, dynamic temporal modeling (93), and interpretable deep multimodal fusion frameworks (94). With continued advances in integrated imaging, ultra-high-field MRI, and AI-assisted systems modeling, heart-brain axis research is expected to progress from static correlation analysis toward mechanism-driven precision medicine frameworks for early detection and personalized intervention in heart-brain comorbidities.

Conclusion
This review highlights that the heart-brain axis is not merely a conceptual framework for qualitative description but a complex cross-organ biological system that can be quantitatively characterized through multimodal magnetic resonance imaging. Collectively, these findings indicate that cardiac and cerebral injuries are more likely to reflect a coordinated systemic pathological process than independent organ-specific events. Nevertheless, current evidence remains largely observational and cross-sectional, limiting the ability to establish causal directionality and temporal dynamics within heart-brain interactions. Future studies integrating longitudinal multimodal MRI, genetic epidemiology approaches such as Mendelian randomization, and advanced causal inference frameworks may help clarify whether cardiac abnormalities precede cerebral degeneration, whether brain dysfunction drives cardiovascular remodeling, or whether both arise from shared pathogenic mechanisms. In addition, the incorporation of dynamic network modeling, graph-based artificial intelligence algorithms, and time-resolved imaging biomarkers may enable more precise characterization of the spatiotemporal evolution of heart-brain coupling across different stages of disease. With continued advances in multimodal MRI data integration, longitudinal modeling, and AI-assisted causal analytics, heart-brain axis research is expected to progress beyond the identification of associations toward the delineation of causal pathways and dynamic interaction patterns between the heart and the brain. Such efforts may uncover critical driver nodes, disease initiation sites, and therapeutic windows of opportunity, ultimately facilitating earlier detection, more accurate risk stratification, and precision intervention strategies for heart-brain comorbidities.

Multimodal MRI can reveal coordinated remodeling of the heart-brain axis at the macroscopic structural level. CMR, currently regarded as the gold standard for assessing cardiac structure, function, and tissue characteristics, enables comprehensive evaluation of ventricular remodeling, myocardial fibrosis, edema, and perfusion abnormalities through techniques such as cine MRI, LGE, and T1/T2 mapping. LGE is widely used to identify focal fibrosis and scar formation, whereas T1/T2 mapping and extracellular volume fraction (ECV) measurements allow quantitative assessment of diffuse myocardial fibrosis and tissue remodeling (13). Correspondingly, structural brain MRI, including T1-weighted and T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging, can detect representative cerebral injury phenotypes such as brain atrophy, cerebral infarction, and white matter hyperintensities (WMHs) (14). An increasing number of studies have demonstrated significant associations between cardiac remodeling and structural brain abnormalities. For example, patients with heart failure frequently exhibit reduced gray matter volume (15) in regions including the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and cingulate cortex, whereas patients with atrial fibrillation (16) or cardiomyopathy frequently exhibit cerebral small vessel disease markers, including increased WMH burden and silent cerebral infarction and manifestations of cerebral small vessel disease (17). These findings suggest that cardiac and cerebral injuries are not isolated events (14) but rather components of a systemic remodeling process jointly driven by chronic hypoperfusion, vascular remodeling, and autonomic imbalance (18).

Therefore, structural MRI is valuable not only for identifying single-organ injury, but also for providing critical imaging evidence to characterize “structural co-remodeling” within the heart-brain axis. This approach is gradually shifting research on heart-brain comorbidities from the description of localized lesions toward cross-organ systemic phenotyping and integrative network-based analysis (19). Current evidence regarding the temporal sequence and causal direction of heart-brain remodeling remains limited. Most available studies are cross-sectional in nature and primarily demonstrate concurrent associations between cardiac abnormalities, such as reduced myocardial strain, ventricular remodeling, and myocardial fibrosis, and cerebral alterations, including white matter hyperintensities, hippocampal atrophy, and disrupted functional connectivity. Beyond macroscopic structural alterations, diffusion MRI further reveals microstructural network injury within the heart-brain axis (21). Techniques such as diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), DTI, and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) enable multidimensional assessment of cerebral microstructural abnormalities, including white matter fiber integrity, axonal density, and neural network organization. The CAN primarily includes the insular cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, thalamus, and brainstem, and is responsible for integrating emotional, cognitive, and visceral autonomic information (22). DTI studies have shown that patients with heart failure and neurodegenerative diseases commonly exhibit reduced white matter integrity within frontolimbic systems and brainstem autonomic pathways (23), characterized by decreased fractional anisotropy and increased mean diffusivity (24). For example, in patients with Parkinson's disease and AD (25), abnormalities in white matter connectivity are associated not only with cognitive decline, but also with reduced heart rate variability and impaired blood pressure regulation (26). Across representative heart-brain disorders, converging multimodal MRI evidence has revealed recurring cross-organ imaging signatures. Abnormal insular functional connectivity is frequently associated with impaired myocardial strain, whereas hippocampal atrophy and white matter injury commonly accompany myocardial fibrosis and adverse cardiac remodeling (39). Acute brain injuries such as ischemic stroke can rapidly induce significant cardiac dysfunction (45), representing a classic brain-to-heart pathological pattern. The underlying mechanisms are primarily related to injury of key autonomic regulatory centers, including the insular cortex, thalamus, and brainstem (46), which triggers a sympathetic storm and catecholamine-mediated cardiotoxicity (45). Acute brain injury also activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (45), leading to excessive catecholamine release. This cascade contributes to neurogenic myocardial injury, myocardial stunning, and microcirculatory dysfunction. In addition, catecholamine surge can disrupt intracellular calcium homeostasis and impair mitochondrial function in cardiomyocytes, ultimately resulting in apical ballooning of the left ventricle, known as Takotsubo syndrome (TTS) (47). This neuro-cardiac interaction is characterized by a dynamic and bidirectional relationship. On one hand, excessive sympathetic activation may further aggravate cardiac injury through neurogenic myocardial edema and inflammatory responses. On the other hand, reduced cardiac output caused by myocardial stunning can exacerbate cerebral hypoperfusion, thereby worsening ischemic brain injury and creating a vicious cycle of injury propagation. Cardiac dysfunction following stroke represents one of the most representative models of acute neurogenic myocardial injury in heart-brain axis research and has recently been conceptualized as stroke-heart syndrome (48). Epidemiological studies have shown that patients with TTS have a significantly increased risk of stroke (49), while the incidence of TTS in patients with acute ischemic stroke is approximately 1.2% (47), suggesting a close bidirectional pathological relationship between the two conditions. In patients undergoing both cardiac and brain MRI, typical imaging features of TTS may coexist with stroke-related cerebral lesions, further supporting the presence of brain-heart coupling (50). The insular cortex, as a key autonomic regulatory hub, may trigger excessive sympathetic activation and myocardial injury when affected by ischemia (46). In addition, brainstem ischemia-related autonomic dysfunction is also considered an important mechanism underlying acute neurogenic cardiac injury. Conversely, cardiac disorders such as atrial fibrillation and heart failure can further increase the risk of stroke and cerebral hypoperfusion, forming a sustained heart-brain pathological cascade (51). MRI plays a crucial role in elucidating stroke-related cardiac injury. Brain MRI, particularly DWI, FLAIR, and perfusion imaging, enables precise delineation of ischemic core and penumbra (52). Lesions involving the insula, thalamus, and brainstem are closely associated with arrhythmias, myocardial injury, and hemodynamic instability, as these regions are directly involved in baroreflex regulation and autonomic output (52). Damage to these structures can rapidly disrupt the balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic activity. Notably, some ischemic stroke patients may present with DWI-negative findings (53), which are generally associated with relatively favorable clinical outcomes. On the cardiac side, CMR can identify characteristic features of TTS (54), including regional wall motion abnormalities, myocardial edema, and the absence of obstructive coronary artery disease. Techniques such as T1/T2 mapping and LGE further enable quantitative assessment of myocardial tissue alteration and microvascular injury. Overall, this brain injury-triggered cardiac response reflects, at its core, catecholamine-mediated neurogenic myocardial toxicity and acute microcirculatory dysfunction occurring on a short temporal scale (48).

Subsequent CMR imaging reveals characteristic manifestations of neurogenic myocardial injury, including left ventricular dysfunction, apical ballooning, and myocardial edema (56). Together, these multimodal imaging findings illustrate the disruption of central autonomic regulation and catecholamine-mediated myocardial injury that underlie stroke-heart syndrome, providing imaging evidence of bidirectional brain-heart interactions.

Heart failure(HF) is a common clinical disease characterized by a decrease in the blood supply of the heart due to anatomical or functional problems with the heart. In China, studies on the epidemiology of HF have revealed an increase in the prevalence rate among people over 35, from 0.9% in 2000 to 1.3% in 2019 (57). Ischemic cardiomyopathy and hypertension are considered major causes of HF and are associated with cognitive function. Decreased systolic function of the heart and blood redistribution are symptoms of HF, which is frequently a subsequent condition to myocardial infarction (58, 59). The fundamental etiology of brain functional injury is thought to be the decrease in cerebral perfusion pressure brought on by decreased cardiac output and inflammation worsened by oxidative stress (60, 61). Although anatomical abnormalities in the brain were linked to biomarkers of myocardial injury and cardiac failure, only older people with poorer cognitive reserves displayed cognitive deficits (62, 63). Conventional MRI is only applicable to lesions with significant brain structure and cannot fully identify the pathological mechanism. White matter hyperintensity (WMH) was connected to sorrow and anxiety, and atrophy of the medial temporal lobe was connected to cognitive problems such as memory loss and executive dysfunction in HF patients. Reduced hippocampal volume is present in HF patients, which may contribute to depression and short-term memory loss (64). fMRI further evaluates neural activity and functional connectivity by measuring blood oxygenation and cerebral blood flow changes, revealing reduced activation in autonomic and cognitive regulatory regions such as the insula, hypothalamus, anterior cingulate cortex, cerebellum, and hippocampus (58), which may contribute to impaired attention, emotional regulation, and working memory in HF. Structural MRI (sMRI), particularly when combined with advanced analytical techniques such as voxel-based morphometry and surface-based morphometry, enables quantitative assessment of gray matter density, cortical thickness, and white matter integrity, demonstrating widespread gray matter loss in the medial temporal lobe, hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and precuneus that correlates with cognitive decline and HF severity (65, 66). In addition, WMH detected on T2-weighted or FLAIR imaging is closely associated with impaired information processing speed and executive dysfunction (67, 68). Cerebral perfusion imaging, including ASL, provides a noninvasive assessment of cerebral blood flow and microcirculation, showing reduced perfusion in the frontal cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, parietal lobe, and cerebellum of HF patients (58), suggesting that chronic cerebral hypoperfusion may contribute to neuronal injury and cognitive deterioration. Overall, the integration of conventional MRI, fMRI, sMRI, and perfusion imaging offers a comprehensive framework for understanding the heart-brain interaction in HF-associated cognitive impairment and may improve early diagnosis, mechanistic exploration, and therapeutic monitoring (15).

Representative multimodal MRI findings of heart failure-associated brain injury and cognitive impairment are illustrated in Figure 4. In patients with heart failure, reduced cardiac output and chronic hemodynamic impairment may result in sustained cerebral hypoperfusion and progressive neurovascular dysfunction. Functional MRI and advanced imaging analyses reveal alterations in large-scale cognitive and autonomic regulatory networks. Compared with controls, patients with HF showed significant ADC changes in multiple brain regions, primarily in the frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes (69). Collectively, these multimodal MRI signatures provide imaging evidence of chronic heart-brain coupling and highlight the impact of cardiovascular dysfunction on cerebral structure, perfusion, and functional network organization.

Neurodegenerative diseases such as AD are characterized by progressive neuronal loss, disruption of large-scale neural networks, and chronic autonomic dysfunction. Increasing evidence suggests that AD is frequently accompanied by cardiovascular abnormalities, including impaired heart rate variability, autonomic imbalance, arrhythmias, and subclinical myocardial dysfunction, indicating chronic remodeling along the heart-brain axis. Research by Aili Toyli and colleagues has increasingly illuminated a complex, bidirectional relationship between cardiovascular disease and AD (70). Unlike acute brain injury-related cardiac dysfunction, neurodegeneration-associated heart-brain remodeling develops gradually and is characterized by chronic neurovascular dysfunction, persistent autonomic dysregulation, cerebral hypoperfusion, and progressive network reorganization. Multimodal MRI provides important insights into the structural, functional, and neurovascular mechanisms underlying these chronic interactions. Structural MRI studies consistently demonstrate hippocampal and medial temporal lobe atrophy in AD (71, 72), often accompanied by increased white matter hyperintensities, suggesting concomitant cerebral small vessel disease and chronic ischemic injury (73). ASL further reveals reduced cerebral blood flow in temporoparietal and posterior cingulate regions, closely associated with cognitive decline. DTI and NODDI show reduced white matter integrity and axonal density, particularly within hippocampal-prefrontal and limbic pathways. fMRI studies further demonstrate disrupted connectivity within the DMN, salience network, and memory-related circuits, with DMN dysfunction considered a hallmark imaging feature of AD. Importantly, DTI and fMRI can detect structural and functional abnormalities before overt clinical symptoms, supporting their value in early diagnosis (74). In addition to cerebral abnormalities, patients with AD frequently exhibit autonomic and cardiovascular dysfunction, including reduced heart rate variability, impaired baroreflex sensitivity, orthostatic hypotension, and altered sympathetic-parasympathetic balance. Chronic autonomic dysregulation may further impair cerebral perfusion and vascular homeostasis, thereby forming a vicious cycle between neurodegeneration and cardiovascular dysfunction. CMR studies also suggest the presence of subclinical myocardial remodeling and impaired cardiac function in some patients with AD (75). Recent advances in multimodal MRI and artificial intelligence have further improved the diagnostic and predictive capability of neuroimaging in AD. The integration of structural MRI, ASL, DTI, rs-fMRI, MRS, and machine learning enables multidimensional assessment of brain atrophy, perfusion deficits, white matter degeneration, metabolic abnormalities, and network dysfunction, providing promising tools for early diagnosis, longitudinal monitoring, and precision intervention in AD-related heart-brain axis remodeling (76, 77).

In neurodegenerative disorders, chronic neuronal loss and progressive disruption of large-scale brain networks may gradually impair autonomic regulation and contribute to cardiovascular dysfunction. Alzheimer's disease provides a representative model of this chronic brain-to-heart interaction, in which structural degeneration, perfusion abnormalities, and functional network disruption coexist with autonomic and cardiovascular alterations. Multimodal MRI enables comprehensive characterization of these cross-organ changes, revealing the complex relationship between neurodegeneration and cardiovascular remodeling (Figure 5) (78–81).

title: Rehabilitation of Women with Neurodegenerative Diseases.
abstract: Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease are 3 prevalent neurodegenerative diseases. Beyond disparate disease incidences between men and women, additional sex-related differences exist. Disease presentation, natural course, treatment considerations, genetic factors, hormonal factors, health care utilization patterns, and outcomes can vary between men and women in general. These disease processes represent examples of well-defined discrepancies between men and women afflicted. Other neurodegenerative conditions, such as motor neuron disorders, progressive supranuclear palsy, and multisystem atrophy, have shown to have a slight predilection toward men compared to women, yet have not been as extensively studied.

title: Cytoskeletal disintegration in cardiovascular disease-related neurodegeneration.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and cognitive decline associated with stroke, have a similar clinical trait involving the alteration of microtubule dynamics and cytoskeletal integrity. The neuronal cytoskeleton is essential for facilitating axonal transport, synaptic connections, and providing structural support. In Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia, tau protein undergoes hyperphosphorylation and dissociates from microtubules, forming insoluble aggregates that obstruct intracellular transport and destabilize microtubule structure. Additionally, region-specific posttranslational changes of tubulin are modified, further impairing cytoskeletal control. In Parkinson's disease, the aggregation of α-synuclein induces oxidative damage and directly impairs microtubule polymerization, especially in the dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra. Stroke induces acute ischemia and reperfusion injury, resulting in surges of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, disruption of the blood-brain barrier, and neuroinflammatory cascades that rapidly destroy cytoskeletal proteins and alter microglial phenotypes. Cardiovascular conditions, including hypertension, heart failure, and atherosclerosis, lead to persistent cerebral hypoperfusion, which promotes progressive neuronal damage and alters tubulin expression and organization. Cardiovascular complications intensify oxidative stress and impair neurovascular coupling, establishing a detrimental cycle that accelerates cytoskeletal disintegration and neural impairment. Collectively, such conditions demonstrate a heart-brain axis in which cardiovascular problems directly lead to microtubule disintegration and dementia. Understanding these pathways provides a unified framework for cytoskeletal biomarkers and novel therapeutic approaches to preserve neuronal structure in various neurological conditions.

title: A quick test of cognitive speed can predict development of dementia in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) patients frequently develop cognitive impairment. There is a need for brief clinical assessments identifying PD patients at high risk of progressing to dementia. In this study, we look into predicting dementia in PD and underlying structural and functional correlates to cognitive decline in PD. We included 175 patients with PD, 30 with PD dementia, 51 neurologically healthy controls and 121 patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) from Skane University Hospital, BIOFINDER cohorts. All underwent cognitive tests, including MMSE, 10-word list delayed recall (ADAS-cog), A Quick Test of cognitive speed (AQT), Letter S fluency, Clock Drawing Test (CDT) and pentagon copying. In non-demented patients with PD, abnormal AQT and CDT results predicted an increased risk of subsequent development of dementia (hazard ratio 2.2 for both). A quick test of cognitive speed can predict development of dementia in Parkinson’s disease

Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients frequently develop cognitive impairment. There is a need for brief clinical assessments identifying PD patients at high risk of progressing to dementia. In this study, we look into predicting dementia in PD and underlying structural and functional correlates to cognitive decline in PD. We included 175 patients with PD, 30 with PD dementia, 51 neurologically healthy controls and 121 patients with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) from Skane University Hospital, BIOFINDER cohorts. All underwent cognitive tests, including MMSE, 10-word list delayed recall (ADAS-cog), A Quick Test of cognitive speed (AQT), Letter S fluency, Clock Drawing Test (CDT) and pentagon copying. In non-demented patients with PD, abnormal AQT and CDT results predicted an increased risk of subsequent development of dementia (hazard ratio 2.2 for both). When comparing the cognitive profile between PD and AD, decreased performance on AQT, which measures attention and processing speed, was more typical in PD. Lastly, we investigated the underlying structural and functional correlates for the PD-specific test AQT with magnetic resonance imaging. In PD patients, decreased performance on AQT was associated with i) cortical thinning in temporoparietal regions, ii) changes in diffusion MRI, especially in the cingulum tract, and iii) decreased functional connectivity in posterior brain networks.

Introduction
Parkinson´s disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease1 and a common cause of motor symptoms, cognitive decline and dementia. The overall prevalence of PD is approximately 1% of the population >60 years of age. It has been estimated that 75% of patients with PD that survive more than 10 years develop dementia with a point prevalence of close to 30%2, although some studies suggest a lower cumulative prevalence of 46%3. The development of dementia is a serious problem that severely worsen the quality of life of patients and their relatives4 and increases the costs for society5.

Accurately predicting and diagnosing PD with dementia (PDD) is not only important for allocating necessary resources and care-giver support6, but also for treating the patients correctly. Randomized clinical trials (RCT) have shown positive cognitive effects of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors7 and memantine8 in PDD. Prediction of PDD may in the future also be valuable for choosing and evaluating neuromodulatory treatments.

Previously, memory and executive impairment has been shown to predict dementia in PD9 as well as impaired pentagon copying10. However, perhaps due to underlying heterogeneous pathologies, predicting dementia in PD remains a challenge, and the underlying pathology needs to be more elucidated.

The three aims of this study were to (1) evaluate the performance of various brief cognitive tests for predicting subsequent development of PD dementia, (2) identify tests specific to the cognitive decline in PD, and (3) examine the underlying brain correlates of the cognitive deficits in PD. First, we studied which cognitive tests could predict development of dementia in patients with PD (n = 175) during a mean of 5.5 (SD 2.3) years of follow-up. Next, patients with PDD at baseline (n = 30) were compared to an independent cohort of AD patients (n = 121) to evaluate which tests were specific for PDD.

Finally, in an attempt to shed light on specific patterns of pathology in PD dementia. we evaluated the underlying functional and structural correlates of declining processing speed in PD with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) modalities, evaluating cortical thickness, white matter tracts and functional connectivity.

Methods
All participants were recruited at Skane University Hospital in southern Sweden and included patients with PD, PDD, AD as well as neurologically healthy controls. The cases are part of the prospective and longitudinal Swedish BioFINDER study (Biomarkers For Identifying Neurodegenerative Disorders Early and Reliably) described in previous publications from our group11 and at http://biofinder.se. This study started in 2008 and is still ongoing. The PD patients met the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke Diagnostics Criteria for PD12. The patients with PDD met the clinical diagnostic criteria for dementia associated with PD according to Emre et al.13. The healthy controls (HC) served as a control group and were neurologically and cognitively healthy. The AD patients met the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (Third Edition Revised) criteria for dementia and the criteria for probable AD defined by the National Institute of Neurological and Communicative Disorders and Stroke-Alzheimer´s and Related Disorders Society14.

The study participants underwent cognitive evaluation according to the proposed algorithm and instruments for establishing the diagnosis of PDD at Level I by Dubois et al.15 and the DSM-V criteria16. The evaluation was performed at baseline and 2nd year for up to 10 years (follow-up range: 1.5–10 years). Conversion to dementia was evaluated at every time point (2, 4, 6, 8 or 10 year), or by chart review in the case of dropouts. A physician with experience in movement disorders performed a detailed history and neurological exam at every visit, as well as a review of the patient’s charts. A research nurse performed the cognitive testing. In this study, MMSE was chosen as the measure of global cognitive function. To measure episodic memory, the 10-word list delayed recall from the Alzheimer´s Disease Assessment Scale – cognition (ADAS-cog) was used17. Phonemic fluency was measured with Letter S fluency18 and visuospatial function with the Clock Drawing Test (Shulman’s scoring method19) and pentagon copying20, scored using the scoring method suggested by Caffara et al.21. Attention and processing speed was measured with AQT22–24. Briefly, AQT is a time trial of naming forms, colours and lastly the combination of coloured geometrical figures. The test aims to measure processing speed and executive function. It is a time trial where the figures are described by form and colour first separately, then in combination. The measured variable is the time it takes to name of 40 colors/forms. Motor function was assessed using UPDRS-III25. All patients were examined in the ON-state. For the longitudinal analysis of clinical progression in the PD cohort, all PD patients (n = 175) that were non-demented at baseline were followed clinically for up to ten years, (mean 5.3, SD 2.3, range 1.5–10). A physician with experience in neurodegenerative disorders evaluated the patients for presence of PDD at baseline or conversion to PDD at every follow up visit, based on clinical test scores and global functioning at home and in society. For dropouts, patients’ medical records were also reviewed for information about conversion to PDD during the follow up period. In the longitudinal analysis, a predefined AQT Color Form cutoff of >80 seconds was used (+2 SD above mean in a reference population26) and a predefined cutoff of <4 points was used for the Clock Drawing Test19.

For investigation of regional brain changes associated with cognitive impairment, we performed MR imaging in 108 cases with PD and 17 cases with PDD. The clinical information closest to the MRI scan was analysed. All MR imaging was performed on 3 T Siemens Skyra MR equipment using the standard 20 channel headcoil. Coronal MPRAGE comprised 180 slices, voxel size 1 × 1 × 1 mm3. The resting state-fMRI protocol comprised 256 T2*-weighted echo planar imaging volumes sensitized to the BOLD effect (echo time 30 ms; repetition time 1850 ms; 33 axial slices; matrix 64 × 64; voxel size 3 × 3 × 3.75 mm3). Subjects were instructed to lie still with their eyes closed, without thinking of anything in particular and without falling asleep. DKI data comprised 99 volumes with 52 continuous slices, three volumes with b = 0 s/mm2 and 96 volumes with b-values of 250, 500, 1000, and 2750 s/mm2, distributed over 6, 6, 20, and 64 directions27. The voxel size was 2.3 × 2.3 × 2.3 mm3 and FOV 294 × 294 × 120 mm3. Motion and eddy current distortions were corrected using an extrapolation-based method for improved high b-value performance. Image volumes were smoothed using an isotropic 3D Gaussian kernel with a full-width at half maximum of 2.3 mm28–30. DKI parameter maps of fractional anisotropy (FA), mean kurtosis (MK), and mean diffusivity (MD)31 were obtained using in-house developed software which fitted the diffusion and kurtosis tensors by nonlinear optimization.

Using the free image analysing tool Freesurfer, available at http://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu, we analysed T1MPRAGE MR images.

Freesurfer software package is a validated tool for measuring cortical thickness32. Non-brain tissue is removed and grey and white matter is separated. The post processing results were quality controlled with visual inspection prior to analysis. Three patients were excluded due to corrupted data. Using the QDEC application in the free Freesurfer software package, we correlated the AQT scores, as well as the results from the other cognitive tests (MMSE, CDT, Pentagon copying, Letter S fluency and Delayed Word recall), to cortical thickness as the dependent variable in a whole brain analysis, using Monte Carlo simulation of 1.3. The model was balanced for age and years of education.

Tractography using deterministic tracking based on constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD) was performed to generate the left and right dorsal cingulum (CG), the hippocampal CG, the corticospinal tract (CST) the fornix (FX), the uncinate fasciculus (UF), the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF), and the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFO)33. One seed-ROI covering the full extent of the specific tract and logical AND- and NOT-ROIs were defined in Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) 152 standard-space and warped back to native-space utilizing the warp-fields generated by FLIRT and FNIRT34. All tracts were visually inspected and ROIs were adjusted in order to secure location of the tract in the intended anatomical region with the number of streamlines below 100. The average parameter estimate for each tract was extracted and used in the subsequent analyses. Since the differences we aimed to elucidate could be relatively subtle, we abstained from a whole brain approach WBA, because of the risk of it being to insensitive considering the multiple comparison issues with such voxel-based approach.

fMRI scans were preprocessed using the Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM8) software (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm). In brief, the following steps were applied: removal of first six volumes, correction for time offsets between slices, realignment, normalization to the MNI template, temporal high-pass filtering (0.01–0.08 Hz), regression of six head motion parameters, and white matter and cerebrospinal fluid signals. To remove the influence of volumes affected by motion, we applied a scrubbing procedure using root-mean-square intensity differences between volumes N to volumes N + 1 with DVARS35. In this study, 1 PD and 2 PDD patients showed head motion > =3 mm translation and rotation, and for this reason they were excluded from the analyses.

Functional brain networks were constructed for each subject using a set of nodes representing brain regions. These nodes were connected by edges representing the statistical interdependence in blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals. The nodes were defined using the 200 cortical and subcortical regions provided by the Craddock atlas36. The edges were calculated as the Pearson correlation coefficients between the regional time series of all possible pairs of regions, resulting in a 200 × 200 correlation matrix for each subject. To assess whether functional connectivity between the previous brain regions was associated with AQT performance, we used the network-based statistic (NBS) software package37.

SPSS 25 was used for all statistical analysis except for the Freesurfer data where the built in application Query Estimated Design Contrast, QDEC, was used38. For comparisons between the different diagnostic groups at baseline (PD, PDD, and HC), a univariate linear model corrected for age, sex, years of education and disease duration was applied with corrections for multiple comparisons using the Bonferroni method. The PD and AD patients were compared with a similar model, corrected for MMSE and age as a measure of global cognitive function and disease burden. For correlation analysis between cognitive tests and tractography, partial Pearson correlations were performed, corrected for age, sex, years of education, disease duration and brain volume. Since these analyses were exploratory in nature, we did not correct for multiple comparisons. For evaluation of the predictive value of cognitive tests on subsequent development of dementia, we performed cox regression analysis corrected for age, sex, disease duration and years of education.

In Freesurfer, the built-in application QDEC was used for analysis. The analysis was adjusted for age, sex, years of education and disease duration. A Monte Carlo simulation was used and p < 0.05 was considered significant. For the functional network analysis, a regression analysis was carried out to test whether AQT scores correlated with functional connectivity in the whole patient group, while controlling for age, sex, education and disease duration. Correction for multiple comparisons was performed using a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.001 (1000 permutations).

All individuals gave their written informed consent. The study procedure was approved by the local ethics committee at Lund University, Sweden, and conducted according to the Helsinki Declaration.

Results

Discussion
In this study, we found that both AQT and the Clock Drawing Test predicted increased risk of developing dementia in PD (HR 2.2). When comparing cognitive profiles between PDD and AD, AQT was more specific to PDD, and we therefore further examined the underlying structural correlates of AQT performance (i.e. declining processing speed) in PD and PDD. We found that poor performance on AQT was associated with cortical atrophy in temporoparietal areas (mainly in the left hemisphere), diffusion changes in certain white matter tracts, mainly the cingulum tract, and decreased connectivity in posterior networks.

A few cognitive tests have previously been shown to predict conversion to dementia in PD. For example, Barker et al. found evidence that both verbal fluency, with a relative risk (RR) of 9.4 (95% CI 1.9–47.5) for a global decline, and inaccurate pentagon copying, with a RR of 5.2 (95% CI 1.9–14.1), predicted dementia in PD39. This could not be replicated in our cohort (Table 2). In the present study, we instead found that AQT and the Clock Drawing Test predicted dementia in PD, but not MMSE, pentagon copying, verbal fluency or word list delayed recall. The prediction of dementia using AQT is in agreement with previous findings showing that conversion to dementia can be predicted with tests of attention and executive function9.

Even though both AQT and Clock Drawing Test predicted subsequent development of dementia, AQT was more specific to the cognitive decline in PDD. When comparing the cognitive profile between PDD and AD, AQT scores were worse in the PDD group, but no difference was seen for Clock Drawing Test scores. As expected, the AD patients performed worse on delayed recall, but delayed recall did not seem to increase the risk of developing dementia in PD, suggesting that decline in episodic memory is not a typical or early feature in PDD. This is in accordance with previous studies showing that the cognitive profile in PD is initially more marked by dysexecutive symptoms and decreasing processing speed40,41, whereas AD patients decline more in episodic memory42,43, even though multiple cognitive domains can be affected in both disorders40,43.

The neuropathology of PDD is complex. Likely, a combination of α-synuclein pathology and AD-like pathology (amyloid-β and tau aggregates) is responsible for the cognitive symptoms44. Which pathology is more important is not fully elucidated45, but some authors suggest that α-synuclein pathology predominates46. It has been suggested that the cognitive symptoms are not solely a result of dopaminergic loss but also cholinergic insufficiency (which is thought to cause attention deficits)46,47, as well as degeneration of other neuronal cell types in the cortex. Previous studies of cortical thickness in different stages of PD have shown correlations between disease stage and cortical thinning48. For example, Zarei et al. found correlations between decreased MMSE and cortical thinning in several cortical areas in PD, including the posterior cingulate and precuneus. In our study, worse AQT scores correlated to decreased thickness in the posterior cingulate cortex as well as in the inferior parietal and temporal areas.

When it comes to structural connectivity, Kamagata et al. found decreased FA values in the cingulum tract in PD and PDD49. In our study we also found weak correlations between decreased processing speed and increased MD values in the cingulum as well as in the ILF and IFO tracts connecting the occipital lobe to the temporal lobe and frontal lobe, respectively50. While other studies have found evidence of frontostriatal involvement in dysexecutive syndromes in PD51, we also found associations between AQT and decreased connectivity in posterior networks and tracts with occipital connections. This could represent deficits in rudimentary visual processing and set-shifting, which is in agreement with the brain regions that are involved during the AQT Color Form task as visualized using fMRI and regional cerebral blood flow measures (rCBF)52.

A limitation of the study is that a larger battery might have identified other predictive tests for dementia conversion in PD, but, nonetheless, our cognitive battery included all tests recommended by the Movement Disorder Society Task Force15 and even some additional ones. The structural MRI findings were considered exploratory in nature, and therefore not corrected for multiple comparisons. Further studies are therefore warranted to confirm these findings. Strengths of the study are the relatively large and well described cohort, the large proportion of the original cohort that underwent MRI, and the long and structured follow-up.

We conclude that the dementia in PD is predominantly characterized by declining processing speed and executive dysfunction, which can be evaluated with the readily available test AQT. AQT can also predict subsequent development of dementia. Using the predefined cutoff of >80 seconds for AQT Color Form, clinicians can identify PD patients who have increased risk of developing dementia. Declining processing speed seems to have structural correlates in the cingulum tract and posterior functional networks. Further studies are needed to develop more precise methods and markers to predict cognitive decline in PD, and to shed more light on the underlying structural basis of cognitive decline in PD.

This is in accordance with previous studies showing that the cognitive profile in PD is initially more marked by dysexecutive symptoms and decreasing processing speed40,41, whereas AD patients decline more in episodic memory42,43, even though multiple cognitive domains can be affected in both disorders40,43.

The neuropathology of PDD is complex. Likely, a combination of α-synuclein pathology and AD-like pathology (amyloid-β and tau aggregates) is responsible for the cognitive symptoms44. Which pathology is more important is not fully elucidated45, but some authors suggest that α-synuclein pathology predominates46. It has been suggested that the cognitive symptoms are not solely a result of dopaminergic loss but also cholinergic insufficiency (which is thought to cause attention deficits)46,47, as well as degeneration of other neuronal cell types in the cortex. For example, Zarei et al. found correlations between decreased MMSE and cortical thinning in several cortical areas in PD, including the posterior cingulate and precuneus. In our study, worse AQT scores correlated to decreased thickness in the posterior cingulate cortex as well as in the inferior parietal and temporal areas.

In our study we also found weak correlations between decreased processing speed and increased MD values in the cingulum as well as in the ILF and IFO tracts connecting the occipital lobe to the temporal lobe and frontal lobe, respectively50. This could represent deficits in rudimentary visual processing and set-shifting, which is in agreement with the brain regions that are involved during the AQT Color Form task as visualized using fMRI and regional cerebral blood flow measures (rCBF)52.

title: TMS and EEG Pharmacodynamic Effects of a Selective Sphingosine-1-Phosphate Subtype 1 Receptor Agonist on Cortical Excitability in Healthy Subjects.
abstract: Current anti-epileptic drugs lack efficacy, cause many side effects and one third of all patients are treatment-resistant. Drugs targeting the sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor show potential anti-convulsant effects in animal models and decrease cortical excitability in patients with multiple sclerosis, but available compounds alter lymphocyte trafficking and cause immunosuppression, limiting their clinical anti-epileptic potential. TRV045 is a selective sphingosine-1-phosphate subtype 1 receptor agonist without effects on lymphocyte trafficking, demonstrating efficacy in animal models of epilepsy, with the potential to target abnormal cortical excitability. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-way cross-over, multiple-dose study evaluated the effects of TRV045 on cortical excitability in healthy male adults, measured by pharmaco-electroencephalography and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Subjects received TRV045 250 mg or placebo, once daily for 4 days, in randomized order. Endpoints were analyzed with a mixed effects model analysis of covariance. Twenty-five of the 27 subjects completed the study. There was a significant increase in alpha power with eyes open after treatment with TRV045 on Day 1, increasing after 4 days of dosing. Less pronounced significant effects in beta, gamma, and delta power were observed after 4 days. For TMS-Electromyography there was a non-significant decreased post-dose single-pulse peak-to-peak amplitude on Day 1 only, and there were no effects on paired-pulse parameters. Several significant TMS-Electroencephalography clusters were seen after 4 days of dosing. These findings show that TRV045 has central nervous system activity with evolving effects following repeated dosing. These data support further studies to elucidate the mechanism of action of TRV045 and its potential anti-epileptic effects.
