Receptor‐mediated transcytosis (RMT) is the only option for transporting molecules from the blood across the BBB (Figure 1). 36 Previous studies have indicated that brain endothelial cells exhibit lower RMT activity than peripheral endothelial cells. Nevertheless, this pathway is promising for drug delivery across the BBB. RMT involves three distinct receptors: insulin, transferrin (Tf), and low‐density lipoprotein. In addition, the roles of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and diphtheria toxin receptors in RMT were described recently. 37 , 38 The RMT mechanism involves three steps: endocytosis, intracellular vesicle trafficking, and exocytosis. Endocytosis is initiated by the binding of molecules to their receptors on the luminal side of endothelial cells. Transport vesicles are formed as a result of the receptor‐ligand complexes invading the cells. Thereafter, the vesicles are sorted for exocytosis, and the ligand is released into the basolateral side of the cell. Finally, the receptor is reused. 39

Apart from transport through the endogenous mechanisms in endothelial cells and other BBB cells, techniques for transient manipulation of the BBB have been explored to enhance drug delivery. Focused ultrasound has been demonstrated to reversibly increase the permeability of the BBB in the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex in humans, with no adverse events detected for up to 17 treatments. 40 Osmolarity manipulation has also been used to increase the permeability of the BBB. Chu et al. 12 demonstrated that intra‐arterial injection of hyperosmotic mannitol in mice could permeabilize the BBB, allowing entry of therapeutic agents. Often, localized application of these techniques requires the use of interventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). 41 Pharmaceutical transient opening of the BBB by disrupting its tight junctions or shrinking endothelial cells using agents such as vascular endothelial growth factor 42 and chlorpyrifos 43 has been reported as well. However, transient opening of the BBB is highly variable and potentially dangerous because it can compromise the integrity of the BBB even after recovery of its permeability status, affecting its physiological function. Furthermore, the use of pharmaceutical molecules can lead to the accumulation of unwanted imaging/guiding (like MRI) or permeabilizing agents in the blood, which may be noxious to the CNS at high levels. Moreover, many of these procedures are invasive, which makes them uncomfortable for patients and increases the risk of adverse events. 44 Owing to these limitations, modifying therapeutic NPs to enhance transport across the BBB and brain uptake is a more attractive approach than transient disruption of BBB permeability."}, {"heading": "IMPORTANCE OF NPS IN DRUG DELIVERY", "text": "NPs are specially designed and synthesized molecules with sizes ranging from 1 to 100 nm. NPs can be grouped into a variety of classes based on their composition, size, or method of action. NPs are composed of metals, often Au, Ag, or Pb, and/or polymers, and can be modified with peptides, lipids, or other biochemical additives for specific functions. NPs are increasingly being favored for therapeutic purposes owing to their customizability; that is, control over their composition, size, and functional groups, which allows for greater specificity, bioavailability, and bioactivity compared to conventional drugs. Furthermore, given that NP coatings allow for control over delivery locations and kinetics, NPs can be tailored to specific patients and diseases. The size and customizability of NPs have made them an increasingly important option for disease treatment. 45 Notably, NPs have been specifically developed to enhance drug delivery for the treatment of NDs.

NPs were developed to enhance the delivery of drugs, including diagnostic agents, to target disease sites and facilitate subsequent release of the drug. In addition, NPs can target specific organs or tissues, 46 including individual cells or intercellular compartments. NPs have an underlying structure integrated with an active drug candidate that allows for angled entry and controlled release of the drug at the targeted site. 47 Traditional modes of drug delivery such as powders, capsules, tablets, or liquids have critical limitations such as high‐dose requirements, short lifetime within the body, and variable pharmacokinetics. However, NPs can successfully transport drugs through the biological acidic milieu with improved permeability, which enables the achievement of maximum efficacy at a relatively low dose. 48 , 49 Considering the physicochemical properties of NPs, even a poorly soluble drug can be effectively translocated to the targeted site to achieve an improved treatment profile. 50 NP‐based technology is considered the best approach to treating diseases due to the myriad of nanomaterials available, which offer numerous positive features for drug delivery strategies. 29 Use of NPs for the treatment of NDs has been gaining attention owing to their improved delivery of drugs and diagnostic agents to diseased target sites and subsequent triggering of drug release.

NPs are characterized by a strong surface adsorption ability. In addition, they have an active center, are highly reactive, and exhibit a high level of catalytic activity. The rates of drug release by NPs can be accurately controlled and modified to improve the therapeutic effects of the delivered drug. Notably, redox effects have been observed in certain NPs, particularly metal and carbon NPs, both in vitro and in vivo. In addition, these NPs have been shown to be potent antioxidants. Antioxidant NPs may be useful as scavengers of reactive oxygen species (ROS). 31 Recent research has proven that NPs can be proactive in bypassing oral and intestinal absorption barriers and delivering drugs to the site of action. This ability can be attributed to the small size of NPs. For instance, drugs with low molecular weights and molecular sizes smaller than 100 nm can pass through the BBB via a diffusion mechanism to avoid phagocytic opsonization, 51 thereby improving their concentration in the brain. Hence, drug‐conjugated nanomaterials have several advantages over modern and traditional bulk materials owing to their special characteristics. 52 The wide range of drug‐delivery properties and therapeutic applications of NPs are discussed in the subsequent sections."}, {"heading": "PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF PD AND CURRENT TREATMENT OPTIONS", "text": "The key pathological findings in PD are loss of dopaminergic neurons in basal cells and appearance of Lewy bodies in cell cytosols (Figure 2). Lewy bodies are formed through the aggregation of abnormally folded proteins called α‐synuclein. The discovery of mutations in the SNCA gene led to the identification of α‐synuclein 53 as the underlying reason for the formation of insoluble aggregates from intercellular inclusions within the cell body and Lewy neuritis of neurons. 54 The pathology of the formation of Lewy bodies extends beyond the brain and can be observed in the spinal cord and peripheral nervous system. 55 It is known that α‐synuclein can form a diverse range of aggregate types, including small, dot, thin, and thread‐like structures. 56 α‐synuclein can also be observed as tiny presynaptic deposits and soluble oligomers that contain 2‐110 α‐synuclein monomers. Although Parkinsonism may be influenced by these different forms of α‐synuclein aggregates, oligomeric protofibrils are particularly toxic to neurons. 57 Abnormal and nonfunctional α‐synuclein are eliminated by the autophagy‐lysosomal pathway, the ubiquitin‐proteasome system (UPS), and molecular chaperones. The PTEN‐induced kinase 1 (PINK1), Parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase (PRKN), protein deglycase‐1 (DJ‐1) and ubiquitin C‐terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH‐L1) genes are typically responsible for regulating the UPS. However, if these genes mutate, mitochondrial and UPS dysfunctions will occur, further leading to the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons. 58 , 59

Molecular pathways involved in the formation of Lewy bodies in Parkinson's disease. The most common pathogenic mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease include mitochondrial dysfunction, proteolysis defects, gene mutations, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. These mechanisms are implicated in the aggregation and accumulation of α‐synuclein, ultimately leading to the formation of Lewy bodies. DJ‐1, daisuke‐Junko‐1; LRRK2, leucine‐rich repeat kinase 2; MPTP, 1‐methyl‐4‐phenyl‐1,2,3,6‐tetrahydropyridine; PRKN, parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase; PINK1, phosphatase and tensin homolog‐induced kinase 1; ROS, reactive oxygen species; UCH‐L1, ubiquitin C‐terminal hydrolase L1.

Molecular pathways involved in the formation of Lewy bodies in Parkinson's disease. The most common pathogenic mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease include mitochondrial dysfunction, proteolysis defects, gene mutations, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. These mechanisms are implicated in the aggregation and accumulation of α‐synuclein, ultimately leading to the formation of Lewy bodies. DJ‐1, daisuke‐Junko‐1; LRRK2, leucine‐rich repeat kinase 2; MPTP, 1‐methyl‐4‐phenyl‐1,2,3,6‐tetrahydropyridine; PRKN, parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase; PINK1, phosphatase and tensin homolog‐induced kinase 1; ROS, reactive oxygen species; UCH‐L1, ubiquitin C‐terminal hydrolase L1.

Oxidative stress is a major event that occurs during aging and directly damages the CNS. Free radicals, or ROS, are essential for apoptosis, gene transcription, host defense, and control of neural plasticity under physiological conditions. 60 Oxidative stress occurs when cellular antioxidant activity is surpassed by the activities of ROS. Enhanced oxidative stress resulting from various mechanisms can deplete lysosomes and damage the lysosomal autophagy system. 61 This indicates that oxidative stress is linked to the accumulation of α‐synuclein. Another hypothesis is that excess cytosolic dopamine can be easily oxidized to produce dopamine‐quinones. Furthermore, chaperone‐mediated autophagy may be partially inhibited by α‐synuclein that has been changed by dopamine quinine, leading to α‐synuclein self‐assembly. 62

An important finding that suggests mitochondrial dysfunction plays a role in the etiology of PD was observed in a study conducted in 1983. 63 1‐methyl‐4‐phenyl‐1,2,3,6‐tetrahydropyridine (MPTP), 64 rotenone, 65 , 66 pyridaben, 67 fenpyroximate, 68 and trichloroethylene 69 infusions have been observed to selectively inhibit mitochondrial complex I. Furthermore, animal studies have indicated that mice that overexpress synuclein are more vulnerable to toxins than mice that lack α‐synuclein, suggesting that mitochondrial synuclein increases toxicity. Transcription factors are major causes of mitochondrial dysfunction. An important regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis is the transcription factor coactivator peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma coactivator‐1a (PGC‐1a). 70 Dopaminergic cells in PGC‐1a knockout mice show increased sensitivity to MPTP. Another hypothesis of mitochondrial dysfunction involves mutations in certain genes, including Parkin, DJ‐1, leucine‐rich repeat kinase 2 and PINK1, which are responsible for mitochondrial and UPS function. 71 , 72 , 73 Mutations of these genes cause mitochondrial dysfunction. Another evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction in PD is the increased mitochondrial DNA levels in tissue samples from patients with idiopathic PD. Recent studies have confirmed an increase in mitochondrial DNA deletions in the brains of patients with PD, particularly in post‐mortem substantia nigra pars compacta tissue. 63 , 74

Ferroptosis, also known as iron‐dependent cell death, is caused by abnormal iron metabolism and severe lipid peroxidation. Oxidative stress and cell death are consequences of iron‐dependent controlled cell death. Ferroptosis has been found to be involved in the death of dopamine neurons in patients with PD. 75 Neuroinflammation is a significant factor in the development of PD. The primary controllers of neuronal loss in PD are microglia, which are associated with chronic neuroinflammatory conditions. In response, environmental factors such as MPTP, rotenone, and 6‐hydroxydopamine, including endogenous proteins, can cause overactivation of microglia and produce ROS, which can cause neurotoxicity. 60

PD causes a range of motor and non‐motor symptoms, including tremors, stiffness, slowness of movement, and balance problems. Its non‐motor symptoms include depression, anxiety, and cognitive changes. Treatment helps improve these symptoms, making the performance of daily activities easier. When patients present with motor symptoms, they are typically recommended treatment options that can improve their symptoms and make engagement in daily activities easier. Pharmacological therapy, physical therapy, rehabilitation therapy, and surgery are the therapeutic options currently used for the treatment of PD. The pharmacological treatments focus on relieving motor and non‐motor symptoms. Seven types of medications are available for the treatment of PD: l‐DOPA, carbidopa, dopamine agonists, 76 , 77 monoamine oxidase‐B inhibitors, 78 injectable dopamine agonists, N‐methyl‐d‐aspartate receptor inhibitors, and anticholinergic drugs. These medications are used to stimulate dopamine receptors or inhibit the breakdown of endogenous dopamine. 79 l‐DOPA acts directly as a dopamine receptor agonist and is stable and effective for treating PD. However, its efficacy diminishes with the progression of PD, leading to the onset of motor dysfunction. 80 Current nanotechnology‐based drug delivery techniques focus on relieving motor symptoms of PD by modulating dopamine signaling in the CNS, either through direct delivery of the agent or stimulation of its receptors.

Apart from α‐synuclein pathology, several molecular pathways related to the aforementioned pathophysiology of PD have been identified as potent NP targets for treatment of PD. These include oxidative processes, such as the mitochondrial calcium pathway and Wingless‐related integration site/beta‐catenin pathways. Other pathways that play pivotal roles in PD progression include the protein kinase B/nuclear erythroid 2‐related factor 2/extracellular signal‐regulated kinase/glutathione pathway, which is involved in antioxidant activity, and the platelet‐derived growth factor receptor signaling/protein kinase B/mammalian target of rapamycin pathway, which is involved in regulation of the cell cycle. Further, the Janus kinase/signal transducers pathway has been found to be highly involved in the immune activation of microglia and astrocytes in the nervous system. By targeting receptors at the beginning of these pathways or intermediate proteins, NPs can modulate important molecular pathways involved in the progression of PD. 81"}, {"heading": "PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND PRESENT TREATMENT OF AD", "text": "The molecular mechanisms underlying the pathology of AD are not fully understood. However, research findings suggest that the amyloid hypothesis explains the primary cause of AD. Paroni et al. 82 separated amyloid β (Aβ) from the brain cortices of patients with AD in 1984. Based on their findings, they suggested for the first time that the accumulation and aggregation of Aβ in the cerebral cortex can cause inherited and non‐inherited AD. 83 This was the first statement on the amyloid hypothesis. In the same year, the authors also discovered that the Aβ amino acid sequence matched the sequence of amino acids extracted from the brain cortices of people with Down syndrome. In 1985, 84 chromosome 21 was discovered at the location of the gene encoding the APP, and in 1987, the APP gene was duplicated at locus 21q21.3. Notably, the amyloid hypothesis has been improved in several aspects since its official declaration in 1992. Aβ deposition is caused by a discrepancy between the production and clearance of Aβ peptide. 82 Gradual accumulation and aggregation of the peptide in the brain is caused by this imbalance, which then leads to a neurodegenerative cascade (Figure 3). 7

Pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease. The image illustrates how amyloid beta, aging, amyloid beta precursor protein cleavage, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurofibrillary tangles are interconnected in molecular pathways to contribute to neuronal cell death and cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease. APP, amyloid beta precursor protein; ROS, reactive oxygen species; Tau, tubulin associated unit.

Pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease. The image illustrates how amyloid beta, aging, amyloid beta precursor protein cleavage, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurofibrillary tangles are interconnected in molecular pathways to contribute to neuronal cell death and cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease. APP, amyloid beta precursor protein; ROS, reactive oxygen species; Tau, tubulin associated unit.

APP is best known as the precursor molecule 80 that is formed through sequential cleavages by β and γ secretase at the C and N terminals of Aβ, respectively. β‐secretase generates the 99‐amino acid C‐terminal fragments of APP. Further cleavage is achieved by γ‐secretase at several sites to create cleavage fragments that consist of amino acids 43, 45, 46, 48, 49, and 51. 85 The main final forms of Aβ, including the 40‐amino‐acid Aβ40 and 42‐amino‐acid Aβ42, are further broken down into endocytic compartments. 86 The Aβ peptide causes serious neurotoxin issues and leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and reactions with metal ions in the brain. 87 In addition, it increases oxidative stress, which disrupts calcium homeostasis by changing calcium ion concentrations. Notably, microglia release inflammatory mediators to cause neuroinflammation due to Aβ exposure. Both Aβ and neurotoxin issues are not mutually exclusive as they can trigger each other. Although such response impedes the metabolism of AAP, it results in the accumulation of Aβ peptides. 88 The accumulation of Aβ peptide initiates hyper‐phosphorylation of tau protein, which is a microtubule‐associated protein enclosed by the microtubule‐associated protein tau (MAPT) gene. 89 Tau proteins are abundant in the CNS, and six isoforms are expressed in brain tissue through alternative splicing of the MAPT gene on chromosome number 17q21. In patients with AD, tau is hypo‐phosphorylated and has extra folds compared to normal tau. Tau protein misfolds and accumulates in paired helical filament tau and neurofibrillary tangles. 90 , 91 , 92 Neurofibrillary tangles may reduce normal tau function, compromise normal cellular function, and finally lead to neurodegeneration. 93 , 94

There are two types of treatment options for AD: Nonmedical and medical. Nonmedical treatments primarily aim to enhance quality of life or preserve the patients' cognitive and daily functioning abilities. The Food and Drug Administration has approved six drugs for the treatment of mild‐to‐moderate AD. 95 However, these medications can only temporarily improve the symptoms of the illness. Moreover, the efficacy of the drugs vary significantly between individuals, with patients often reporting side effects such as nausea, diarrhea, and vomiting. 96 Two of these medications, aducanumab and lecanemab, are of a highly pursued class of AD therapies, Aβ‐targeting monoclonal antibodies. Aβ‐targeting antibodies work by binding to Aβ plaques. This binding transforms the plaques into a soluble form, breaking them down and triggering opsonized phagocytosis by glial cells. Both of these antibodies have been demonstrated to decrease Aβ pathology and AD‐associated cognitive deficits in animal models and attenuate Aβ pathology in clinical trials. However, although both antibodies have demonstrated moderate therapeutic effects and an ability to decrease Aβ levels, they have failed to exhibit “clinically significant” benefits in patients with prodromal dementia. In fact, approximately 1.3% of the participants in the EMERGE and ENGAGE clinical trials who were treated with aducanumab developed amyloid‐related imaging abnormalities. 97 Nevertheless, amyloid‐targeting antibodies represent an important culmination in research on the amyloid hypothesis. Further evaluation and improvement of the efficacy of these treatments could position amyloid‐targeting therapeutics as an attractive future treatment option for amyloid‐based dementias. 98 The limitations of the existing therapies highlight the urgent need for alternative therapies for AD. The role of the BBB must be considered in the development of effective treatments for AD. Nanotechnology has significant potential in the development of drug delivery systems with various functional carriers, such as peptides and polymers, that can to alter the properties of drugs to enhance their therapeutic potential for the treatment of AD. 99

In addition to Aβ and Aβ precursor proteins and other protein aggregates such as tau, recent research has identified additional targets for NPs and other therapeutics. These include proteins that control amyloid production and aggregation, such as the medin, bassoon, and pseudoautosomal regions. Recent studies have demonstrated that the pathological forms of these proteins are oligomeric. Thus, oligomeric Aβ and tau may be more specific targets for NPs than previously anticipated. Further, neuroinflammation is increasingly being associated with the incidence and progression of NDs. Thus, NPs and drugs delivered in NPs can be designed to promote an anti‐inflammatory state, such as by incorporating sigma‐1 receptor ligands or by promoting an anti‐inflammatory state in microglia, which are the immune cells of the brain. Research on neuroinflammation‐based therapeutics is currently in the very early stages; however, targeting cytokine receptors, release of cytokines, and other state‐controlling pathways may have potential in the use of NPs for neuroinflammation‐based treatment of AD and PD. 98"}, {"heading": "PEPTIDES IN DRUG DELIVERY", "text": "Many biological processes require the crucial roles of proteins and peptides, such as catalysis, transportation, regulation of genetic expression, and immune functions. Proteins and peptides have diverse functions and are involved in many pathological conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, and cancer, making them appealing therapeutic agents for the treatment of these diseases. Currently, there are more than a hundred approved, peptide‐based, therapeutic products in the market. The peptide and protein drug market is growing much faster than that of small‐molecule drugs. This is because peptides and proteins can be very selective as they have several points of interaction with the target. 100

Engineered NPs encapsulated in peptides and proteins that target drug delivery to the brain have been researched in recent decades. Currently, there are a variety of peptides and proteins that are only focused on a small class of receptors, such as low‐density lipid receptors, Fc‐like growth factor receptors, leptin receptors, receptor‐associated proteins, insulin receptors, scavenger receptor type B1, a cell surface receptor, and Tf receptor. 101 Given that these receptors are mostly present in the BBB, receptor‐mediated drug delivery is an important approach to the treatment of AD and PD. 102 Peptides and proteins have been developed as ligands for specific receptors to increase the efficacy of transport across the BBB. NPs encapsulated in peptides and proteins have unique features such as high diversity, specificity, and targeting capability. Therefore, they are used as innovative drug delivery agents for the treatment of AD and PD. 103

The rabies virus glycoprotein‐29 (RGV‐29) is a specific kind of peptide can particularly recognize nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (Table 1). It is not only expressed in endothelial cells but also in astrocytes, microglia, and dopaminergic neurons. Therefore, rabies virus protein 29 encapsulated NP formulations can achieve successful drug delivery to PD lesions. 104 Angiopep‐2 is an oligopeptide that contains 19 amino acids and binds to the low‐density lipoprotein receptor‐related protein‐1 (Table 1). 106 Angiopep‐2 has been encapsulated in different types of nanostructures to effectively deliver therapeutic agents for the treatment of AD and PD. NPs modified with the B6 peptide can accumulate in brain capillary endothelial cells via lipid rafts and clathrin endocytosis (Table 1). B6 has a unique characteristic in that it is capable of dual drug delivery; it is non‐cytotoxic to the mouse hippocampal neuronal cell line (HT‐22) and can cross the BBB both in vitro and in vivo. 108 Tet methylcytosine dioxygenase 1 (Tet‐1) is a peptide with twelve amino acids that was identified by Mathew A et al. 109 through phage display (Table 1). Tet‐1 has transport properties and an affinity for neurons and is used to deliver curcumin, epigallocatechin‐3‐gallate, and small interfering RNA for the treatment of AD. 109 The authors observed a longer lifetime within the blood and greater penetration of the BBB using cyclic Cys‐Arg‐Thr‐IIe‐Gly‐Pro‐Ser‐Val‐Cys (CRT) peptide and conditionally releasable CD47 modified NPs, allowing for more efficient delivery to microglia. RMT has been used to develop long‐circulating delivery drugs, such as dopamine for AD and huperzine for PD, to target certain organs (Table 1). 111

Envelope protein of the rabies virus was developed by the addition of four glycine and nine d‐arginine residues to the C‐terminus peptide and is used to deliver small interfering RNA for the suppression of the α‐synuclein gene involved in the development of PD (Table 1). 113 Human apolipoprotein E (ApoE) receptor‐binding domain is the source of the peptide cysteine‐tryptophan‐glycine‐77, and can be modified by adding the tri‐peptide cysteine‐tryptophan‐glycine at the C‐terminal for the delivery of phosphatidic acid for the treatment of AD (Table 1). 114 The heptapeptide H2N‐Gly‐l‐Phe‐d‐Thr‐Gly‐l‐Phe‐l‐Leu‐l‐Ser(O‐beta‐d‐Glucose)‐CONH2 (g7) has tyrosine at the N‐terminal end and is O‐glycosylated (Table 1). Several in vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that g7 effectively transports polyethyleneglycol‐polylactic acid‐co‐glycolic acid NPs into the brain, indicating its potential for the treatment of AD. 115 , 116 The most commonly used cell‐penetrating peptide is Tat peptide, which is used to target AD. Tat peptide contains twelve amino acids and is derived from the protein transduction domain of the human immunodeficiency virus (Table 1). 125

Lactoferrin (Lf) is a natural glycoprotein with iron‐binding properties that is present in large quantities in colostrum and breast milk. In addition, Lf receptors are overexpressed in brain capillary endothelial cells. Owing to the abundance of Lf in these cells, it has been found to be a perfect nano‐carrier for certain drugs such as dopamine and rotigotine for the treatment of PD, and huperzine for the treatment of AD. 126 , 127 The single peptide chain of Tf is a monomeric co‐protein found in blood serum and other human fluids. Tf receptors are expressed in animals, some insects, and bacteria. Tf‐modified liposomal NPs are used for the delivery of ApoE2 for the treatment of AD. 118 Serum albumin is a single‐chain non‐glycosylated, specific structural polypeptide with specific binding sites for a variety of endogenous and exogenous drugs, and is considered the best nano‐carrier for the treatment of AD and PD. 128 Keratin, a protein derived from human hair, has a rich disulfide bond that can be broken in a high‐level reduction environment. In addition, the amino acids in keratin can be protonated in acidic conditions, resulting in pH sensitivity, which bestows the characteristics of dual pH and glutathione responsiveness on the protein. Therefore, keratin is used as a dopamine delivery system in the treatment of PD. 124"}, {"heading": "PEPTIDE/PROTEIN‐CONJUGATED POLYMERS USED IN DRUG DELIVERY FOR THE TREATMENT OF AD AND PD", "text": "Polymeric NPs (PNPs) are particles made of polymers with sizes ranging from 1 nm to 1000 nm. 129 Degradable NPs are increasingly being utilized for the delivery of drugs for the treatment of NDs, owing to their high loading capacity, ability to permeate the BBB to reach the CNS, 130 minimal toxic properties, and controllable degradation timeline and degrees. 131 PNPs are block copolymers composed of naturally occurring monomers, such as polysaccharides and albumin, as well as synthetic monomers. They are easily excreted, biodegradable, and largely biocompatible, and thus suitable for human biological applications. 132 Polymeric nano‐capsules are another form of polymer NPs in which the drug is encapsulated in the internal cavity created by a polymer coating. 133 Like PNPs, polymer‐based NPs vary in retention time, solubility, and biological availability, making them attractive options as therapeutic agents. However, the nature of the interactions between the polymer and the drug should be considered in applications of encapsulation. If the interaction between the polymer and drug is more dominant than the interactions between the molecules of the drug, the drug can be stably incorporated into NPs. However, if the drug–drug interaction is stronger, drug crystallization occurs. To optimize the balance of these interactions, various natural polymers, such as albumin, 134 alginate, 135 gelatin, 136 and chitosan, 77 and synthetic polymers such as poly (lactic‐co‐glycolic) acid (PLGA), 137 , 138 poly (lactic acid), 139 poly (caprolactone), 140 , 141 poly (butyl cyanoacrylate), 142 , 143 , 144 and poly‐l‐lactic acid, 145 are being tested for medical applications. Use of PNPs is one of the most promising and modern strategies for delivery of therapeutic drugs to the brains of patients with AD. The superior internal distribution and pharmacokinetics of these agents hold great promise for improving the efficacy of drug delivery. The most commonly selected polymers for the synthesis of NPs are chitosan, albumin, poly (butyl cyanoacrylate), poly (lactic acid), PLGA, polyethylene glycol, and polyethylenimine. These polymers contain moieties that facilitate the formation of three‐dimensional nanonetworks through covalent cross‐linking with other motifs of the same polymer backbone, leading to single polymer‐based or single‐chain polymer NPs. 146 In addition, the polymers react with other polymers to form heterogeneous NPs. Groups that are not utilized for the assembly or synthesis of the NPs can be employed for functionality, including controlled release and localization of drugs. Drugs can be restricted from being released through many chemical interactions, including steric hindrance such as covalent bonding or attachment to the surface of the NP, allowing for versatile dispersion and absorption of drugs. 147 In addition to temporal control, various chemical gating and attachments allow the release of drugs to specific areas of the brain. These functional modifications allow for efficient loading of drugs, as well as controlled release and selective targeting of specific cell types or brain regions. 148

Fan et al. 108 designed a novel NP, poly (lactide‐co‐glycolide)‐block‐poly (ethylene glycol) (PLGA‐PEG), which they conjugated with peptide B6, loaded with curcumin (PLGA‐PEG‐B6/Cur), and administered to HT‐22 cells and APP/PS1 Al transgenic mice (Table 2). The developed NPs were subjected to in vitro tests, including dynamic light scattering, flow cytometry red blood cell lysis, and thromboelastographic analysis. A result from another study suggested that the PLGA‐PEG‐B6/Cur NP exhibits high biosafety and availability and can be used to treat β‐amyloidosis and tau pathology. Comparison of APP/PS1 mice treated with the NP with mice that received a curcumin treatment demonstrated that the NP treatment improved spatial learning and memory in the disease model. In addition, ex vivo analysis of samples from these mice, including immunostaining, western blot analysis, and Bielschowsky silver staining, demonstrated that PLGA‐PEG‐B6/Cur can reduce the deposition and formation of β‐amyloid as well as hyperphosphorylation. Furthermore, behavioral and biochemical tests revealed the ability of the PLGA‐PEG‐B6/Cur NP to serve as an a therapeutic agent for AD, augmented by the increased delivery to the brain by the PLGA‐PEG‐B6 formulation. 108

Liu et al. 149 developed B6‐modified PEG‐PLA NPs as an effective drug delivery system for improving neuroprotective drug delivery across the BBB for the treatment of AD (Table 2). The ability of the B6 peptide to increase the localization of the NPs in the brain was studied using real‐time imaging. After the NPs were labeled with 1,1′‐dioctadecyl‐3,3,3′,3′‐tetramethyl indotricar‐bocyanine iodide and injected in veins in the tails of mice, the fluorescence of the B6‐NPs lasted longer in the brain than that of the unmodified NPs at all timepoints from 0.5 to 12 h following administration. In fact, the fluorescence of the B6‐NPs was higher than that of the other NPs 1 h after administration, and greater accumulation of B6‐NPs than the unmodified NPs was observed in vivo. At the cellular level, B6‐NP demonstrated endocytosis via lipid rafts and clathrin mechanisms, resulting in significantly high accumulation in endothelial cells. The B6‐NPs were encapsulated in the neuroprotective peptide Asp‐Ala‐Pro‐Val‐Ser‐IIe‐Pro‐1 (NAP) to generate an NP for treatment of AD. When B6‐NP was administered to AD mouse models, NAP mice showed reduced learning disabilities, hippocampal neuron death, and cholinergic signaling disruption, even at low doses. 149

In another study, Bi et al. 120 proposed lactoferrin‐modified PEG‐PLGA NPs as an adjunct to rotigotine for the treatment of PD (Table 2). Cellular uptake of the Lf‐NPs in human bronchial epithelial cells (16 HBE) and SH‐SY5Y cells demonstrated higher accumulation of the Lf‐NPs than unmodified NPs. Intranasal administration of rotigotine to the brain was heterogeneous, yet more effective with Lf‐NPs. Specifically, the Lf‐NPs were highly concentrated in the striatum. Given the susceptibility of striatal neurons to degeneration, this finding suggests that Lf‐NPs allow for the delivery of rotigotine to the most relevant areas in the brain for the treatment of PD. 120

Vilella et al. 116 studied the effects of elevated brain zinc levels on AD pathology in mice treated with g7‐NPs‐Zinc (g7‐NP‐Zn). The authors developed zinc‐containing NPs and performed in vivo studies using wild‐type and APP23 mice to assess plaque burden, inflammatory status, and synapse loss. After 14 days of chromic injections, the mice showed significantly fewer pro‐inflammatory cytokines and smaller plaque sizes. No negative behavioral consequences of elevated brain zinc levels were observed in the APP‐23 mice. In addition, the g7‐NP‐Zn treatment normalized the observed hyperlocomotion in the APP23 mice (Table 2). 116

Huang et al. 112 designed PLGA NPs by coating the amyloid beta generation inhibitor S1 peptide and curcumin to target deleterious factors in patients with AD using the brain‐targeting conjugation CRT peptide (Table 2). The authors assessed spatial memory and recognition using object recognition and Y‐maze tests and found that treatment with the PLGA NPs improved these skills in transgenic AD mice, while simultaneously reducing the amount of ROS and pro‐inflammatory cytokines, including necrosis factor‐alpha and interleukin‐6. In addition, these NPs increased the levels of protective indicators, including superoxide dismutase, and synaptic activities in the mice. Coating with the CRT peptide showed the most favorable treatment of AD compared to other S1 and curcumin‐delivering PLGA NPs. 112 Yan et al. 117 presented an intranasal strategy mediated by PLGA‐modified cell‐penetrating peptide NPs for the delivery of insulin to the brain to treat AD. The authors performed a cellular reception efficacy test using Caco‐2 cells. In addition, they performed fluorescence‐activated cell sorting analysis and reported that Tat‐NPs greatly increased the efficacy of intracellular insulin delivery, showing 4.5 times more accumulation compared with unmodified NPs. Confocal imaging also confirmed the greater intracellular accumulation of insulin. The results indicated that when administered nasally, Tat‐NPs can deliver insulin to the brain with an overall efficacy of 6%. 117 Monge‐Fuentes et al. 123 studied dopamine‐loaded albumin/PLGA nanosystems in 6‐hydroxydopamine ‐induced PD mice models and revealed that at the highest dose, dopamine encapsulated in albumin/PLGA nanosystems significantly improved neurobehavioral symptoms (Figure 4). The improved symptoms included motor coordination, sensory‐motor performance, and balance. In addition, the results indicated that 20 mg of aluminum chloride phthalocyanine can both deliver and replenish dopamine in a manner that translates to tangible effects on PD symptoms. 123

Dos Santos Rodrigues et al. 118 designed liposomal NPs that can protect the ApoE2 plasmid from nuclease degradation (Table 2). A Tf‐modified liposome surface‐penetrating agent effectively induced ApoE expression in vitro by delivering plasmid DNA to the gene. When tested in vivo, the Tf‐penetratin liposome was able to induce ApoE expression in the brains of mice compared to nontargeted preparations. These results demonstrate the great potential of liposomes for the delivery of plasmid DNA and their applications in the treatment of NDs, including AD. 118 Guo et al. 150 developed double‐PEG‐modified single‐walled carbon nanotubes with Lf on their surfaces (SWCNT‐PEGs‐Lf or CAR), which transport dopamine to the brain. Treatment of parkinsonian mice with 25 mg/kg of CAR and dopamine reduced the levels of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (interleukin‐1b, tumor necrosis factor‐α, and ROS), while increasing the density of the immunoreactive tyrosine hydroxylase. Analysis of the doses of CAR and DA that elicited lower oxidative stress and pro‐inflammatory responses following intraperitoneal injection revealed that 25 mg kg‐1 dopamine on 3.25 mg/kg CAR can rescue the aforementioned features in parkinsonian mice. 150

In another study, Zhang et al. 110 demonstrated the process of Aβ aggregation and disaggregation of amyloid fibrils through attachment to epigallocatechin‐3‐gallate (EGCG) to the surface selenium NPs (epigallocatechin‐3‐gallate @ selenium [EGCG@Se]) (Table 2). They further synthesized EGCG‐stabilized selenium NPs coated with Tet‐1 peptide (Tet‐1‐EGCG@Se, a synthetic analog of sialoprotein), with respect to the affinity of Tet‐1 peptide to neurons (Figure 5). The results of the study showed that Tet‐1‐EGCG@Se can inhibit Aβ fibrillation while disaggregating toxic Aβ fibrils. Moreover, the authors found that both EGCG@Se and Tet‐1‐EGCG@Se can label Aβ fibrils and Tet‐1 peptides, increasing uptake of Tet‐1‐EGCG@Se in PC12 cells. 110 Tang et al. 121 prepared NPs co‐modified with borneol and Lf and loaded them with dopamine using a double‐emulsion solvent evaporation method. The results of in vitro cytotoxicity studies suggested that treatment with dopamine borneol and Lf co‐modified NPs (Lf‐BNPs) is not significantly cytotoxic to SH‐SY5Y and 16HBE cells (Table 1). The authors also found that the Lf modification increased the uptake of NPs by SH‐SY5Y and 16HBE cells, whereas addition of borneol promoted uptake by 16HBE cells. The results also indicated that the Lf‐NPs had a significantly higher area under the curve from 0 to 12 h than dopamine NPs. Intranasal administration of dopamine effectively attenuated 6‐hydroxydopamine‐induced Lf‐BNP lesions in the striatum of rats, as indicated by the results of a contralateral rotation behavioral test and the detection of striatal monoamine neurotransmitter content. In addition to the previously discussed NPs, intranasal administration of dopamine Lf‐BNPs is an effective method for improving the symptoms of PD. 121

The therapeutic potential and physical properties of NPs are determined by their monomer composition and preparation process. Many synthetic and natural polymers have been used for the synthesis of protein and peptide nanosystems. The high activity, circulation time, specificity, and low toxicity of these polymer–protein systems make them ideal candidates as nanocarriers. However, the development of polymer–protein hybrid systems is still faced with some challenges. Polymeric nanomaterials must be evaluated and modulated to minimize in vivo toxicity, which can be affected by their physical properties, such as chemical composition, shape, and size, their biochemical properties including agglomeration, surface properties, and their biological properties, such as biocompatibility and biodegradability. In addition to the use of organic solvents, covalent or noncovalent modifications can change the structure of a protein. Therefore, conformation and activity of the protein should be determined during the synthesis procedure to confirm the feasibility of the method. Recent developments in polymer chemistry research involved the reconstruction of synthetic processes and applications of polymer NPs. This has led to the successful development of several new formulations of therapeutic peptides with suitable sizes and surface chemistries. The interaction between the peptides and polymer backbones can be adjusted by considering more factors in the preliminary preparation step. Drug release kinetics can be adjusted and controlled, and the initial burst of drug release can be prevented. Peptide encapsulation of drugs and relevant stabilizing agents in polymer nanosystems can significantly improve peptide stability during formulation and delivery. The rational design of peptide‐conjugated PNPs should involve deep modifications of the sophisticated physicochemical properties of the biological systems and target areas. However, it should be noted that delivery of a pharmacologically active peptide is challenging. Future research should be focused on safe and effective noninvasive administration of PNPs in biological systems. In addition, cooperation and interaction among researchers in various fields, such as chemistry, materials science, biology, and medicine, will enable informal development of versatile polymer NP conjugates to overcome the limitations of the existing therapeutic options.

Peptide‐modified NPs can be further modified to enable visualization of the particles following treatment. Particles may be fluorescently labeled through covalent or noncovalent attachment of a fluorescent molecule to the NP. Fluorophores, such as fluorescent quantum dots, which are especially bright, have narrow/specific emission spectra, and are very photostable, can be encapsulated inside NPs. Furthermore, Forster resonance energy transfer techniques can be used to detect interactions between NPs and their microenvironments through pH‐ or distance‐dependent energy transfer. In addition, NPs can be radiolabeled to detect particles via isotope decay. Some radioactive isotopes can be covalently attached; however, many are immobilized on the surface of NPs, which poses a risk of detachment from the particle following intake. NPs can also be radiolabeled without a chelator through de novo synthesis by adding radioactive precursors during the synthesis of inorganic materials, allowing for incorporation from the beginning. Alternatively, chemical adsorption, in which NPs adsorb radioactive ions from the solution onto their surfaces, can be performed. Finally, non‐metallic NPs can be labeled with metals using various techniques, to enable detection through various imaging techniques, including MRI and transmission electron microscopy. Metal tags can be incorporated onto the surfaces and cores of NPs, allowing for detection without interference with the function of the NP or its interaction with other molecules. 152"}, {"heading": "CONCLUSION", "text": "The number of individuals with NDs has been increasing in recent decades. Despite several research developments, the existing treatments for AD and PD are not effective because of gaps between research findings and proper implementation in clinical settings. The ability of nanotechnology‐based therapeutic agents to selectively target the brain has provided an innovative way to treat these diseases more specifically and efficiently. Recent advances in nanotechnology offer new ways of boosting research on the delivery of targeted drugs to specific sites in the brain. title: Mitochondrial DNA editing: Key to the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Neuronal death is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA. Mitochondrial DNA becomes damaged when processes such as replication, repair, and nucleotide synthesis are compromised. This extensive accumulation of damaged mitochondrial DNA subsequently disrupts the normal function of mitochondria, leading to aging, degeneration, or even death of neurons. Mitochondrial dysfunction stands as a pivotal factor in the development of neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Recognizing the intricate nature of their pathogenesis, there is an urgent need for more effective therapeutic interventions. In recent years, mitochondrial DNA editing tools such as zinc finger nucleases, double-stranded DNA deaminase toxin A-derived cytosine base editors, and transcription activator-like effector ligand deaminases have emerged. Their emergence will revolutionize the research and treatment of mitochondrial diseases. In this review, we summarize the advancements in mitochondrial base editing technology and anticipate its utilization in neurodegenerative diseases, offering insights that may inform preventive strategies and therapeutic interventions for disease phenotypes.

Mitochondrial dysfunction stands as a pivotal factor in the development of neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Recognizing the intricate nature of their pathogenesis, there is an urgent need for more effective therapeutic interventions. In recent years, mitochondrial DNA editing tools such as zinc finger nucleases, double-stranded DNA deaminase toxin A-derived cytosine base editors, and transcription activator-like effector ligand deaminases have emerged. Their emergence will revolutionize the research and treatment of mitochondrial diseases. In this review, we summarize the advancements in mitochondrial base editing technology and anticipate its utilization in neurodegenerative diseases, offering insights that may inform preventive strategies and therapeutic interventions for disease phenotypes.

Introduction
Mitochondria are essential organelles for the normal functioning of eukaryotic cells and play a key role in cellular activities including apoptosis, calcium homeostasis, signal transduction, and regulation of reactive oxygen species levels.1 The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria originated from aerobic bacteria phagocytized by primitive eukaryotic organisms, forming a symbiotic relationship with the host cell.2 Most of the DNA of the original bacterial endosymbiont has been lost or transferred to the nucleus, leaving a much smaller circular molecule, now known as mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA).3 While distinct from the nuclear genome, mtDNA interacts with it and is indispensable for maintaining mitochondrial function.4 Upon exposure to external or internal stimuli, mitochondria undergo perturbations in crucial processes, including mtDNA replication, repair, and nucleotide synthesis, ultimately disrupting mtDNA homeostasis. This disruption significantly impacts neurons, characterized by their high-energy demands and limited regenerative capabilities.5 Recent studies have emphasized the critical role of mitochondria in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), particularly the impact of mtDNA mutations on the development of Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD).6

Given the significance of mtDNA mutations in numerous diseases, researchers have sought ways to mimic or repair these alterations. However, the intricate double membrane structure of mitochondria poses a formidable obstacle for traditional DNA editing tools, particularly CRISPR-based systems.7 To overcome this limitation, mitochondrial gene editing technologies have emerged as promising alternatives. Nuclease-based mtDNA editors, such as mitoZFN and mitoTALEN, have demonstrated the ability to penetrate mitochondria and perform targeted double-stranded cleavage of mutant mtDNA molecules. While these tools effectively alter the mutant/wild-type mtDNA ratio, they are limited in their capacity to mimic or repair specific mutations.8 In contrast, mitochondrial base editing technologies (e.g., DdCBE) can specifically target the repair of mutated mtDNA and drive the transition from the heterogeneous state to a healthy wild-type mtDNA population.9 Based on these advancements, we hypothesized that mitochondrial base editing technology may provide a new direction for the prevention or treatment of NDDs. In this review, we discuss recent advances in mitochondrial gene editing technology and explore the relationship between mtDNA mutations and four common NDDs, aiming to inform the prevention of NDDs or the treatment of disease phenotypes.

Mitochondrial genome and mutations
Mitochondria contain a separate genome, and the full sequence of the mitochondrial genome was determined by Anderson et al in 1981.10 Human mtDNA is a double-stranded circular DNA (dsDNA) molecule containing 16,569 bp with light (L) and heavy (H) strands, each of which can be transcribed. mtDNA is intronless and polycistronic, and its genes encode 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs, and 13 polypeptides that are components of the electron transport chain.11

mtDNA differs from nuclear DNA in that it does not follow the Mendelian laws of inheritance, since mitochondria in a fertilized egg originate almost exclusively from the mother. Consequently, mtDNA is maternally transmitted to offspring.12 In addition, mtDNA exhibits a higher mutation rate than nuclear DNA due to several factors. Firstly, its proximity to the inner mitochondrial membrane exposes it to potentially damaging conditions. Secondly, the lack of protection from histones and DNA-binding proteins makes it highly susceptible to free-radical attack. Lastly, mtDNA lacks an efficient repair system and protective mechanisms to counteract these threats, further contributing to its increased mutation rate. Therefore, mtDNA is prone to mutations.13 Heterogeneity is present in mitochondria when both mutant and wild-type sequences coexist. In such heterogeneous mitochondria, a damaged phenotype manifests only when a specific proportion of mutant mtDNA is surpassed; this is known as the “threshold effect".14 Thus it is only necessary to reduce the proportion of mutated mtDNA below the disease threshold to restore the clinical phenotype, a property that gene therapy exploits (Fig. 1).15Figure 1Manipulating “thresholds” with mitochondrial gene editing tools. If the mtDNA mutation reaches a certain threshold, mitochondrial function becomes abnormal, and oxidative phosphorylation becomes impaired. This blocks cellular energy production and causes the cell to lose viability due to an insufficient energy supply, which may lead to organismal senescence. Recent studies have shown that the increase in aging-associated mtDNA mutations is not caused by the accumulation of damage but by the clonal amplification of mtDNA replication errors that occur during development.16 Lokesh et al knocked down the mtDNA polymerase γ (PolgA D257A) in mice, causing the mice to accumulate mtDNA mutations as they aged. They observed that the mice developed mitochondrial bioenergetic defects, amyloid accumulation, and brain atrophy.17 The causal relationship between mtDNA and aging remains unclear, however, there is increasing evidence that somatic mtDNA mutations are elevated in age-related disorders such as AD, PD, and Huntington's disease (HD), particularly in the brain tissue of affected individuals.18

Mitochondrial gene editing
In recent years, gene therapy technology has developed rapidly, particularly the CRISPR/Cas9 system, which can conveniently cleave DNA in the presence of guide RNA (gRNA).19 However, its application in mtDNA editing is still controversial, mainly for the following reasons: (i) the mitochondrial genome is relatively small and lacks sufficient CRISPR-editable sites; (ii) CRISPR relies on gRNAs for effectiveness, but there is no efficient method to introduce gRNAs into mitochondria.20 Currently, mitochondrial gene editing techniques are based on two approaches: nuclease-based approaches and base editing approaches. Mitochondrial gene editing tools
Artificial nuclease-mediated mitochondrial gene modification technologies (e.g., mitoZFN and mitoTALEN) are highly programmable, specific, and flexible.21,22 ZFNs comprise zinc-finger proteins and the restriction endonuclease FokI. The zinc-finger protein consists of 3–6 ZF modules, with each ZF module recognizing and binding to a 3-bp DNA sequence.23 Transcription-activator-like effectors nucleases (TALEN) are gene editing tools derived from plant pathogenic bacteria. TALE is obtained from the bacterium, xanthomonas, with amino acid sequences corresponding to nucleotide sequences on the target DNA.24 TALE consists of four modules, and one modular unit recognizes one base, which is the key site for specific recognition of DNA.25 TALEN and ZFN are pure protein systems that can achieve targeted cleavage of mtDNA by adding mitochondria target sequence (MTS).21,26 It has been demonstrated in a mouse model carrying a pathogenic mutation in mtDNA (m.5024C > T) that the delivery of mitoZFN or mitoTALEN using AAV9.45 effectively reduces the level of mutant mtDNA and increases the wild-type mtDNA in various tissues such as heart and skeletal muscle.26,27 The effectiveness of artificial nuclease editing systems in targeted editing of mtDNA has been preliminarily demonstrated in in vitro and in vivo studies.

Artificial nuclease editing systems can specifically target and remove mutant mtDNA from heterogeneous cells and induce changes in mtDNA heterogeneity. mitoZFN has a rather low editing efficiency, and an iterative editing strategy requires a long time. Moreover, each of the zinc-finger protein groups binds to 3 bp of DNA, which may cause potential inaccuracies. TALE can recognize individual bases and thus has more flexible site selectivity, however, its arrays are more complicated to analyze and construct and need to be constructed from scratch every time the sites are replaced, which places a great burden on researchers and even makes it difficult to obtain effective structures.28 Therefore, the exploration and development of safer and more efficient gene delivery vectors is crucial for advancing gene therapy research targeting mtDNA. The emergence of such novel vectors is expected to significantly enhance the precision, efficiency, and safety of gene editing, thereby opening new possibilities for gene therapy for mtDNA-related diseases.

The CRISPR-Cas9 system is a widely used genome editing tool.29 The core mechanism lies in the ability to precisely induce double-strand breaks in specific target genomic regions, and realize the editing and modification of the target genome through intracellular DNA repair mechanisms, such as non-homologous end-joining, microhomology-mediated end-joining, and homologous recombination.30 The CRISPR-Cas9 system has effectively overcome the limitations existing in traditional technologies such as TALEN and ZFN. This is due to its user-friendliness and high degree of flexibility, opening up new paths for research and application in the field of gene editing.31 The successful application of the CRISPR/Cas9 system for mitochondrial gene editing was first reported in 2015, demonstrating its feasibility for mtDNA editing in mammalian mitochondria.32 To further explore its function and application in mitochondria, the researchers have modified and optimized the CRISPR system to achieve its efficient translocation to mitochondria and precise manipulation of mtDNA.33 Bian et al showed specific targeting of mtDNA by the mito CRISPR/Cas9 system, leading to the reduction of mtDNA copy number in human cells and zebrafish.34 Bi et al developed the mito-Cas9 system by adding mitochondrial targeting sequences and 3′ untranslated regions of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes upstream and downstream of Cas9 genes, achieving effective degradation of mtDNA, which provided direct evidence to demonstrate the feasibility of the CRISPR-Cas9 system in mtDNA editing.35

There is still a heated academic debate about the applicability and efficiency of the CRISPR-Cas9 system in editing mtDNA.36 Although many studies have confirmed the ability of the CRISPR-Cas9 system to target mitochondria, the efficiency of the mito-Cas9 system in achieving gene knock-in is significantly low. This inefficiency phenomenon is hypothesized to be attributed to two aspects: the lack of mitochondrial translocation efficiency of the editing system, and the limitation of the mtDNA editing ability of Cas9 proteins.35 To improve the editing efficiency of the mito-Cas9 system, future research may focus on two directions: first, optimizing the mitochondrial transport mechanism to enhance the efficiency of the editing components entering the mitochondria; second, developing Cas protein variants with higher editing efficiency through genetic engineering.37 In summary, through continuous research and exploration, the mito-Cas9 system has the potential to be an efficient knock-in strategy and provide novel therapeutic avenues for the treatment of inherited mitochondrial diseases.

Nuclease-mediated gene editing mainly eliminates specific mutant mtDNA, but it cannot correct mutant genomes.38 Base editors are double-strand break-free gene editing technologies that open up new possibilities for precise manipulation of mtDNA. This technology can directly substitute individual bases in DNA, mainly cytosine base editors, adenine base editors, and guanine base editors (Fig. 2).39 Base editors have demonstrated low off-target and low insertion-deletion rates in nuclear genome engineering applications, resulting in increasing interest in the application of this technology to mitochondrial DNA. Mok et al36 found that double-stranded DNA deaminase toxin A (DddA) could edit mitochondrial genes by catalyzing the C-to-T transition in dsDNA. To avoid toxicity, DddA is divided into two parts: DddAtox-N and DddAtox-C. TALE was used to identify target sequences, and a uracil glycosylase inhibitor was introduced to improve the editing efficiency (Fig. 2A). The final synthesized protein, named DddA-derived cytosine base editor (DdCBE), was used to model disease-associated mtDNA mutations in human cells, resulting in changes in respiration rates and oxidative phosphorylation.

Compared with nuclease editing systems, DdCBEs have a wide targeting range, high editing efficiency, and high specificity. Silva et al used an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector to implant DdCBE into the hearts of adult mice via tail vein injection. Editing efficiencies of 2 % and 20 % were detected in mouse heart tissue at weeks 3 and 24 after injection, respectively.43 In addition, DdCBE-mediated mitochondrial base editing is also feasible in human 3 PN embryos, suggesting that it can correct pathogenic mtDNA mutations in the early stages of the human embryo.44 Recently, Pinheiro et al constructed a base editor library (mitoKO) based on the ability of the DdCBE system to knock out all protein-coding genes in the mouse mitochondrial genome, which will provide a basis for subsequent studies of mitochondrial function and the construction of mtDNA gene inactivation model.45

However, when targeting mitochondrial genes in cells, DdBCEs may lead to off-target mutations, which may be due to the spontaneous assembly of DddAtox hemimolecules splitting in the absence of a TALE-DNA interaction.46 In addition, the editing efficiency, editing type, and bystander effect of DdCBE still have many shortcomings that need to be improved.47 Therefore, researchers have developed many strategies to continuously improve the specificity of DdCBEs and to facilitate their application in basic research and clinical trials of diseases. For example, DdCBEs are fused to nuclear export signals (DdCBE-NES) to avoid off-target C-T transitions in the nuclear genome and to improve mtDNA editing efficiency.48 Other optimization strategies, such as modifying the deaminase DddAtox to improve its fidelity, co-expressing repressor proteins of DddA, or modulating the subcellular localization of DdCBEs can also be used to effectively reduce the off-target activity of DdCBEs, laying the groundwork for the application of these tools in gene therapy.37,49

Compared with TALE, ZFNs are small and can be easily packaged in viral vectors for in vivo research and gene therapy applications. Simultaneously, ZFPs are somewhat friendly, and the split DddAtox can be fused to either end of the ZFP. In addition, ZFPs with intrinsic cell-penetrating activity may allow nucleic acid-free gene editing in human cells.50 Therefore, Kim et al38 attempted to fuse DddAtox with specific ZFPs to develop zinc finger deaminases (ZFDs) that catalyze C-to-T base transitions in target DNA and do not induce unwanted insertion and deletion mutations in human cells. The authors successfully improved the gene-editing efficiency of ZFDs by optimizing the linker length, spacer sequence length, and DddAtox splitting site. To deliver ZFDs to the mitochondria, MTS and nuclear export signal sequences were ligated to the N-terminus of ZFDs to form mitoZFDs (Fig. 2B), whose mitochondrial editing efficiencies were in the range of 2.6% to 30% in HEK293T cells. Although ZFDs have achieved relatively high base editing efficiencies in DNA, their relatively low editing efficiencies in mtDNA may limit their application in the treatment of certain mitochondrial diseases. In the future, it is expected that editing efficiency, especially in mtDNA, will be further improved by optimizing design and technology.

While DdCBEs are limited to C-to-T base editing, Cho et al created a novel gene-editing platform called transcription activator-like effector ligand deaminases (TALEDs), which enabled A-to-G conversion for the first time. TALEDs were created in this study by fusing TALE, TadA8e, and DddAtox, each of which plays a distinct role (Fig. 2C).51 TALE is capable of targeting DNA sequences. TadA8e facilitates the A-to-G transition, and DddAtox improves the DNA accessibility of TadA8e. The designed TALED was highly efficient in human cells, catalyzing A-G conversion at 17 target sites across a variety of mitochondrial genes, with an editing frequency of 49%.40

TALEDs are non-toxic, have a low off-target risk, largely reduce the bystander effect, and do not lead to mtDNA instability. Furthermore, to reduce off-targeting and improve the efficiency of mitochondrial editing, researchers have further optimized DdCBE and TALED.52 The introduction of high-fidelity mutations in DddA and the addition of nuclear export signal sequences to DdCBE and TALED have broad implications for basic research and therapeutic applications.53

Wei et al42 proposed a mitochondrial DNA base editor (mitoBE), in which mitoBEs integrate nickase, deaminases, and uracil glycosylase inhibitors under the guidance of the TALE system. Nickase MutH or Nt.BspD6I(C) cleaves the DNA strand at the target site, generating transient single-stranded DNA, which provides an efficient substrate for deaminases (Fig. 2D). Deaminases, in turn, convert A to G or C to T via deamidation, named mitoABE and mitoCBE, respectively, which enables targeted editing in the human mitochondrial genome, providing a powerful tool for generating mitochondrial disease models or correcting most mitochondrial disease-causing point mutations.

MitoBEs, as a novel mitochondrial single-base editing tool, have lower off-target risks and a higher degree of specificity than DdCBEs. This continues to be explored and optimized in depth. Initially, Wei et al, through mutagenesis studies of nicking enzymes, such as MutH, discovered a substantial expansion of the editable sequence range, achieving a more than 10-fold increase. Furthermore, they investigated more effective delivery methods employing circular RNA-encoded mitoBEs, which enhanced editing efficiency and durability across diverse cell types. Future endeavors may involve the design of an expanded repertoire of nicking enzymes to target various mtDNA sequences or the exploration of novel delivery systems, such as nanoparticles, for the precise localization and enhanced editing efficiency of mitoBEs.

Delivery systems for mitochondrial gene editing
To function in vivo, these gene tools require safe and efficient mitochondria-targeted gene delivery systems that protect them from degradation and overcome extracellular and intracellular barriers, particularly the mitochondrial membrane barrier. Currently, MTS-modified, nanoparticle-based, and viral vector delivery systems are the most common and effective strategies for mitochondrial gene editing.

The MTS peptide is labeled in the gene editing tool and crosses the mitochondrial bilayer membrane using the mitochondrial protein uptake mechanism, thus facilitating the efficient entry of the editing tool into the mitochondria and realizing the precise editing of mtDNA.54 The mitochondrial gene editor composed by MTS has been described in detail above. MTS solves the problem of exogenous proteins, such as zinc finger proteins and TALE, not being able to enter the mitochondria, however, there remains the phenomenon of off-targeting of the nucleus, which needs to be further optimized and researched.55 MTS-modified vectors may be cytotoxic, especially as non-specific interactions with the mitochondrial membrane can disrupt mitochondrial membrane integrity. Future designs should optimize the vector or use biocompatible materials to reduce cytotoxicity and non-specific membrane interactions.

Viruses, which have evolved to overcome multiple physiological barriers in the body, have become primary vectors for targeting cells using gene-editing drugs. Most gene-editing drugs use AAVs, whereas some use lentiviruses or adenoviruses. Preclinical studies in mice have shown that AAV vectors delivering mitoZFN or mitoTALEN monomers can successfully achieve heterogeneous transfer.26,27 DdCBE targeting the ND4 and ND1 loci was packaged by AAV, and 99.1% and 59.8% efficient editing were detected 6 days after the transfection of HEK293FT cells.56 However, AAV vectors also have a limited packaging size of less than 5 kb, and this limits the size and efficient delivery of gene editing tools.57 Achieving clinically relevant human doses necessitates impractically high and potentially unsafe titers of AAV vectors, posing a significant challenge for their application in clinical settings. Moreover, when delivering mtDNA editing tools via AAV, considerations include capsid immunogenicity, neutralizing antibodies, and immune responses to AAV-encoded transgenes. Thus, developing novel AAV serotypes with low immunogenicity is crucial for the clinical use of AAV-mediated mtDNA modification tools.58

Non-viral vectors are relatively safe as novel delivery systems with low cytotoxicity and immunogenicity. Lipid nanoparticles are popular non-viral vectors with promising applications in mitochondrial gene therapy; however, they have not yet been used for this purpose. Another type of non-viral vector, virus-like particles, is also showing promise for delivering gene editing tools.59 Notably, virus-like particles have a much larger capacity than AAVs (which are limited to 4.3 KB). This means that lipid nanoparticles can carry more complex, diverse, and precise gene-editing tools for the safe delivery of multiple drugs.58

Challenges of mitochondrial gene editing
The development of mitochondrial gene editing tools has enabled the manipulation of mtDNA and the treatment of mitochondrial diseases. However, the mitochondrial bilayer hinders access to exogenous editing tools, and the high variability of mtDNA copy numbers makes precise editing challenging. Improving gene editing tools can significantly enhance the efficiency and precision of mitochondrial gene editing. For example, the TALED editing tool has achieved an editing efficiency of up to 49 %. However, there is still a need to develop safe and controllable vectors for efficient in vivo delivery to promote mitochondrial gene therapy.

Off-target effects are important in the clinical application of genome-editing tools. A notable example is the research involving DdCBE. Although DdCBE achieves precise mitochondrial editing, it simultaneously triggers extensive single-nucleotide variant off-target effects on the nuclear DNA.47 Given this, editing tools need to be optimized to enhance their base-specific editing ability for mtDNA to improve the precision of mitochondrial gene editing and effectively reduce the risk of off-target editing.

Mitochondrial gene editing enables the treatment of mitochondrial diseases by reducing the intracellular proportion of mutant mtDNA molecules. However, the long-term application of mitochondrial gene editing may affect the dynamics of the cellular proportion of mutant mtDNA molecules, and intracellular mtDNA population dynamics are critical for mitochondrial disease therapy. In addition, long-term mitochondrial editing may lead to undesired mutations in mammalian mitochondria that clonally expand to dangerous levels, thereby affecting mtDNA repair mechanisms.58 In this regard, attempts can be made to circumvent this problem using mathematical models to predict the optimal nuclease dose and heterogeneous transfer efficiency.60 The long-term impact and safety of these editing technologies must be fully assessed, and comprehensive ethical evaluations must be conducted before they transition from the laboratory to the clinic.

mtDNA and neurodegenerative disease
The pathogenesis of NDDs is complex and diverse, and our understanding of NDDs is limited to their pathological features. With the development of gene-editing technology, a large number of NDD-associated mutations and single-nucleotide polymorphism loci have been identified, providing new perspectives for explaining the mechanisms of NDD progression. Genetics is a well-recognized determinant of outcome in common NDDs; however, gene mutations do not explain 100 % of NDD cases and the presence of disseminated cases, even in HD, which is usually regarded as an autosomal dominant disorder.61

In the study of NDDs, much less is known about mitochondrial genetics than about their genetics. However, mtDNA genetics have a potential role in the progression of injury-related NDDs (Fig. 3).62 Mitochondria are closely associated with oxidative stress and play an important role in maintaining functional homeostasis in the brain and in meeting neuronal energy demands. Much evidence suggests that mitochondria play a central role in NDDs associated with aging and that both mutations in mtDNA and oxidative stress promote aging, which is the greatest risk factor for NDDs.63 Mitochondria, like the nucleus, have separate DNA and genes encoding oxidative phosphorylation-related proteins in mtDNA. Mutations in mtDNA occur throughout life due to oxidative damage or errors in mtDNA polymerase, and the clonal expansion of these mutations leads to cellular dysfunction and the production of large amounts of reactive oxygen species, which promotes the development of NDDs.64 It has been demonstrated that mtDNA mutations have been shown to play a role in the development of PD and AD. PD is an age-related degenerative disease of motor neurons.66 As PD progresses and is prolonged in its course, neuronal loss becomes more extensive and can even lead to dementia and hallucinations.67 According to studies, the main pathological factors leading to PD include degenerative death of dopamine neurons in the intracranial substantia nigra,64 α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress.68 In addition, mtDNA alterations play a key role in the progression of PD.69,70 Currently, the main types of mtDNA mutations that may be associated with PD include point mutations, deletions, and regulation of nuclear genes.71,72

It was shown that the age-related increase in oxidative mtDNA damage is associated with age-related impairments of the components of the mitochondrial BER machinery (OGG1, UDG, APE1, and polymerase γ).73 Furthermore, studies have shown that the dysregulation of mtDNA homeostasis is a key process in the pathogenesis of neuronal loss in PD.74 For example, Christian et al found that mtDNA deletions and copy number regulation, rather than point mutations, were the main determinants of mtDNA damage in human neurons. It was also found that in the context of PD, the dynamic regulation of mtDNA copy number is weakened, leading to the depletion of the wild-type mtDNA library, which may contribute to mitochondrial respiratory defects in neurons.75 Another study found that multiple mtDNA deletions accumulated in the substantia nigra became more pronounced with age. This has been associated with nuclear genes encoding proteins associated with mitochondrial maintenance, such as the gene encoding Pol-γ, POLG.76 Other nuclear genes associated with impaired mtDNA maintenance, such as c10orf2 and MPV171, have also been detected in other studies of PD.77,78 Mitochondrial dysfunction can also be caused by mitochondrial epigenetic changes. A recent review highlighted that mitochondrial epigenetics might play an important role in the development and progression of PD and should receive more attention. Mechanistic modulation of the epigenome also appears to be critical for the pathogenesis and progression of PD.48 Blanch et al detected methylation deletions at mtDNA CpG and non-CpG sites in the nigral striatal D-loop region of PD patients. Methylation may regulate mtDNA replication and may be associated with mtDNA deletion as well.79

Several studies have developed gene therapy approaches specifically for PD.80, 81, 82 However, none of these approaches have targeted the underlying pathophysiological features of PD. This is because the unique features of the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, and the interaction between the two have been implicated in the pathogenesis of PD. A combination of different gene therapies may be the most effective treatment strategy.83 We suggest that targeted mitochondrial gene therapy may offer opportunities for treating PD and advance the field of PD gene therapy.

AD is a common neurodegenerative disorder. It is caused by the loss of neurons in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus, aggregation of β-amyloid (Aβ), and neurofibrillary tangles, leading to neuronal degeneration and death.84 Oxidative stress associated with mitochondrial dysfunction is another potential factor contributing to the pathogenesis of AD by inducing the conformational dysregulation of proteins, particularly α-synaptic nucleoprotein, Aβ, and tau.85 Several studies have shown that mitochondrial DNA changes play a key role in the pathogenesis of AD. Currently, the main types of mtDNA mutations associated with AD include deletions, point mutations, and methylation.

mtDNA mutations play a crucial role in AD-related mitochondrial dysfunction. Using ultrasensitive next-generation sequencing to measure the mutational load of the mitochondrial genome, results have shown a significant increase in the frequency of mtDNA mutations in the hippocampus of individuals with early AD.86 In addition, Krishnan et al found that high levels of mtDNA deletion led to COX deficiency, and they observed an increase in mitochondrially biochemically deficient neurons in the hippocampus of sporadic AD patients with COX deficiency.87,88 Further studies have shown an association between the T→C transition in the gene encoding the COX III subunit and reduced citrate synthase activity, with up to 15% of AD patients exhibiting this specific mtDNA point mutation.58 Recent studies have successfully detected mitochondrial epigenetic alterations in the central nervous system, cerebrospinal fluid, and periphery.89 In particular, mtDNA methylation emerges as one of the key factors that may regulate mitochondrial pathology in AD. Blanch et al found increased mtDNA methylation at both CpG and non-CpG sites within the D-loop region of the inner olfactory cortex in AD patients with Braak stages I-II and III-IV versus controls.63 In another study, the D-loop region was demethylated and the mtDNA copy number was reduced in APP/PS1 mice, an animal model of familial AD.90 Collectively, these findings suggest that mtDNA has significant potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target for AD.

Although mtDNA plays a key role in the pathogenesis of AD, there are no relevant studies on targeting mitochondrial genes for treating AD. Currently, CRISPR/Cas9 technology can target the editing of genes associated with AD pathogenesis, such as APP, PSEN1, and APOE, to reduce the production of harmful proteins or increase the expression of protective proteins.91,92 The combination of CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing tools with targeted mitochondrial gene editing technology holds great promise, as it may allow for a more comprehensive approach to treating AD by addressing both nuclear and mitochondrial genetic factors that contribute to the disease. While challenges such as efficient delivery and minimizing off-target effects remain, future research efforts focused on the integration of these technologies hold the key to unlocking new avenues for the prevention and treatment of AD.

HD is a degenerative disease of the central nervous system, characterized by cognitive decline, psychiatric disorders, and motor dysfunction. Its main pathological manifestation is the significant absence of spiny projection neurons in the striatum, a crucial component of the extrapyramidal system. This neuronal loss, being extensive, results in impaired limb motor function.93 HD is an autosomal dominant disorder primarily caused by the amplification of the CAG trinucleotide repeat sequence within the Huntington's disease gene (HTT), ultimately leading to the production of mutant Huntington's protein (mHTT), which structurally differs from its normal counterpart.94 Mitochondrial dysfunction has been found in the brain and peripheral tissues of patients diagnosed with HD.
